cards.status_note: The checked author sources distinguish the open generalized question from the solved ordinary star-height problem. A later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no verified height-two example or universal height-one theorem. The inspected factor-counting results establish additional height-one subclasses only.

context_blocks.text: Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)^{*}\), with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma *ab\Sigma *)^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma^{*}\) by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet \(\{a\}\), the even-length language \((aa)^{*}\) has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes \(x^{N}=x^{N+1}\) for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.

cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(\mathrm{L}_{0}a_{1}\mathrm{L}_{1}\cdots a_{r} \mathrm{L}_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(\mathrm{L}_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(\mathrm{L}(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(\mathrm{L}(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.

context_blocks.text: Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA^{*}\) says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The question defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. cards.context:
Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA^{*}\) says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The question defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, on every pair \((G,H)\) of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether \[\operatorname{Tree}(G)=\operatorname{Tree}(H)?\] Both schemes may have arbitrary finite type order, with their orders supplied by their finite descriptions. Equality is exact equality of the possibly infinite ordered value trees, including the nullary divergence symbol \(\bot\). No safety or productivity promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
A ranked alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of terminal symbols with ranks \(r(a)\in\mathbb N\). Simple types are finite expressions generated by a base type \(o\) and the arrow constructor \(\tau\to\sigma\), associating to the right. A terminal of rank \(r\) has the type with \(r\) arguments of type \(o\) and result \(o\); rank zero means type \(o\). A scheme has a finite set of typed nonterminals, one distinguished start nonterminal \(S:o\), and exactly one rule \[F x_1\cdots x_k\longrightarrow t\] for each nonterminal \(F:\tau_1\to\cdots\to\tau_k\to o\). Here the distinct variables \(x_i:\tau_i\) are the only variables allowed in \(t\), and \(t:o\) is a finite well-typed applicative term over terminals, nonterminals and these variables. Terms are symbols or applications \(uv\), with \(u:\alpha\to\beta\) and \(v:\alpha\) giving \(uv:\beta\); application associates to the left. Rules may be mutually recursive and may duplicate or discard parameters. There are no data tests, constructor equations, pattern matching or nondeterministic alternatives. No syntactic restriction called safety is required.

Starting at the closed ground term \(S\), expose the head constructor by repeatedly replacing a fully applied head nonterminal \(F u_1\cdots u_k\) by \(t[u_1/x_1,\ldots,u_k/x_k]\). When a terminal head \(a u_1\cdots u_{r(a)}\) is exposed, output a node labeled \(a\) with the ordered child trees obtained in the same way from the ground terms \(u_i\). If the head unfolding never exposes a terminal, output a single \(\bot\) node with no children. In particular, unfolding does not require finishing a constructor's arguments before exposing that constructor. This defines \(\operatorname{Tree}(G)\) over \(\Sigma\cup\{\bot\}\). A node address is a finite sequence of positive integers specifying successive child positions, starting with the empty address at the root. A terminal of rank \(r\) has precisely children numbered \(1,\ldots,r\), and \(\bot\) has none. Equality means the same set of addresses and the same label at every address. The number of unfolding steps and the names of internal nonterminals are not observable.

Type order is defined by \(\operatorname{ord}(o)=0\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(\tau\to\sigma)=\max\{\operatorname{ord}(\tau)+1,\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\}\). A scheme's order is the maximum order of its nonterminals; the two input orders need not agree. An input explicitly lists the finite alphabet and ranks, type syntax trees, nonterminal symbols, start symbols and rule syntax trees, with binary indices and delimiters. Well-typedness and the syntactic conditions are effectively checked; invalid descriptions are rejected. The sought machine must work uniformly over all valid encodings, alphabets, finite orders and rule sizes. It returns an exact Boolean answer, without approximation, random error, an oracle, or any additional time or space requirement beyond termination.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability of the input language defined above. A positive answer must supply one effective algorithm and prove its termination and correctness on every valid pair, including equal infinite trees and divergent schemes, uniformly in the finite input orders. A negative answer must prove that no total computable decider exists; undecidability for one fixed order already suffices for this unrestricted problem. A positive algorithm only for a restricted order or safety class, model checking of one tree, or a theorem conditional on another unresolved decision problem is not a full positive answer. No finite-depth approximation to tree equality is accepted.
cards.why: This is a central comparison problem for finite programs with higher-order recursion. Their complete output can be an infinite tree, and strong logical properties of each individual tree are already decidable. Deciding equality would establish an effective method for identifying identical observable recursive behavior across different finite descriptions; undecidability would locate a fundamental boundary beyond single-program verification.

importance.reason: Exact behavioral equivalence for unrestricted finite higher-order recursive descriptions.

progress.text: Sénizergues’s deterministic pushdown equivalence theorem yields the order-one decidability boundary. Jochems’s later discussion states the equivalence between the two order-one formulations.

Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre establish effective translations between higher-order recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata. The final journal-paper discussion explicitly retains equality of two value trees as open.

Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre’s revised work develops effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for these generated structures. These are results about logical properties, not a general tree-equality algorithm.

Jochems gives an equality-preserving treatment of divergence and a conditional equivalence-decidability theorem. The required coinductive-Horn semidecidability remains unresolved, and §5 explicitly calls scheme equivalence open.
The higher-order polyregular preprint proves undecidability for extensional functional equivalence with list operations. Its model and compared objects differ from the deterministic value trees here.

The LICS probabilistic-verification paper establishes almost-sure termination decidability for a type-restricted probabilistic subclass, without deciding unrestricted deterministic scheme equivalence.

The 2017 open passage, the 2021 definitions and conditional theorem, and the scopes of the 2026 neighboring results were checked. A bounded subsequent-work search found no matching resolution; this is a source-status assessment with stated limits.

The April 2026 polyregular and July 2026 probabilistic results concern different models or properties. context_blocks.text: A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule \(S\to a S\), for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system \(S\to a T\) and \(T\to a S\) describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. The question asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation \(plus(0,x)=x\). Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule \(S\to S\) generates ⊥, while \(S\to a S\) generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme \(S\to b S c\), with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, generated trees have finite-state descriptions and equality is decidable. At order one, equivalence is interreducible with deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. The higher-order setting permits functions as parameters of recursive definitions. Jochems’s §5 explicitly distinguishes this unresolved general problem from the established order-one result.

Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre prove that recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata describe the same classes of trees, with effective translations at each order. A collapsible pushdown automaton has a nested stack structure with links allowing restoration of earlier stack contents. The paper transfers value-tree equality to language equivalence for deterministic machines of this kind, but its final discussion explicitly leaves that comparison problem open. Equivalence of two representation models does not itself decide equality of two represented objects.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems’s 2021 result is a conditional decidability theorem: a specified semidecidability property of coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses would imply decidability of scheme equivalence. These clauses describe relations using higher-order logical rules with a greatest-model interpretation. The required semidecidability remains an assumption in Theorem 4.1, so the paper does not provide a completed equality algorithm.

The same paper proves that allowing explicit divergence leaves does not change the decidability question: its transformation to divergence-free trees preserves and reflects equality. Divergence is part of the semantics of an arbitrary input scheme, with no productivity promise. A productive infinite tree and a computation that never exposes a constructor remain distinct outputs.

The April 2026 polyregular result proves undecidability for equality of functions at higher-order types in a calculus with list operations and extensional semantics over function arguments. The paper’s language has no recursion and its programs terminate. Its comparison problem is different from equality of closed, possibly infinite constructor trees generated by the recursion rules here; no reduction between the two problems is assumed.

The July 2026 probabilistic-verification result decides almost-sure termination for a type-restricted class of probabilistic recursion schemes. That is a question about a termination probability in a restricted model. It does not settle equality of deterministic value trees at arbitrary finite orders.

cards.title: Parity games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input length defined below?
cards.definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(L\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.

context_blocks.text: The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(L+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

cards.context:
The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(L+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

The 24 June 2026 revision of Suilen and Pérez’s paper, marked accepted at CONCUR 2026, continues to describe polynomial-time parity-game solving as open. Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That later treatment does not itself refute the 2025 algorithm claim; the current status remains explicitly unverified.

cards.title: Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
cards.definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.

context_blocks.text: Every individual term of the sequence is effectively computable from the finite input, and the existence of a zero is semidecidable: positive instances have a finite witnessing index. The unresolved demand is a procedure guaranteed to finish on zero-free inputs too. The problem concerns the whole class of input sequences; undecidability would not mean that the zero question for each particular named recurrence is unanswerable.

The same recurrence describes linear dynamics in \(k\)-dimensional integer space. With \(v_t=(u_t,\ldots,u_{t+k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), let \(B\) have ones just above the diagonal, zeros in the other entries of its first \(k-1\) rows, and last row \((c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1})\). Then \(v_{t+1}=Bv_t\), including when \(k=1\). The question is whether this orbit reaches the hyperplane where the first coordinate is zero. This makes the connection to exact reachability and termination guards in linear programs explicit.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem says that the zero indices form a finite union of arithmetic progressions, together with a finite exceptional set. Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the question. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem here.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.

cards.why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.

importance.reason: A canonical exact arithmetic reachability problem underlying many verification reductions.

Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the question. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem here.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.

cards.title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
cards.formal: Is the first-order theory of the standard real exponential field \(\mathbb R_{\exp}=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\exp)\) decidable? Precisely, does there exist one ordinary deterministic Turing machine \(D\) which halts on every encoded first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in this fixed language and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_{\exp}\models\varphi\), and \(0\) otherwise? The exponential function is defined on all real numbers, and the required conclusion is unconditional.
cards.definitions: The domain is the standard field \(\mathbb R\), with its usual constants, addition, unary additive inverse, multiplication and strict order. Equality is a logical symbol. Here \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), the standard real exponential, with \(0!=1\); it is not an input function or an oracle available to the machine. Terms are finite expressions formed from variables \(v_i\), \(i\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), the constants \(0,1\), unary negation and exponentiation, and binary addition and multiplication. Atomic formulas are term equalities or strict inequalities. Formulas are formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction and the quantifiers \(\exists v_i\) and \(\forall v_i\). Every quantifier ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\), regardless of the index \(i\); indices name variables, not integer-valued inputs. Binding has its usual nested scope, with the nearest enclosing quantifier on a given variable binding that occurrence. A sentence is a formula with no free variables, and truth uses the ordinary real operations and ordinary first-order semantics. Arbitrarily many variables, nested exponentials and arbitrary finite quantifier alternations are allowed. There are no names for arbitrary real parameters, integer predicates, trigonometric functions or additional input operations. For a fixed finite-alphabet encoding, write a variable as v[b], where b is the usual binary expansion of its nonnegative index, with no leading zero except for the index zero itself. Use literal strings 0 and 1 for constants, and the prefix term forms -(t), exp(t), +(t,u) and *(t,u). Formula forms are =(t,u), <(t,u), not(phi), and(phi,psi), or(phi,psi), exists(v[b],phi) and forall(v[b],phi), with the indicated parentheses and commas and no spaces; t,u stand for terms and phi,psi for formulas, not literal tokens. Thus all inputs are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet of these characters. To make D total on all strings, malformed encodings and formulas with free variables must be rejected with output 0. D has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, has no oracle, noncomputable real constant, advice or random choices, and is the same machine for every input length, number of variables and quantifier pattern. No running-time or space upper bound is imposed beyond halting.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a single total deterministic Turing machine exists and has the stated exact truth behavior, or a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of true encoded sentences is undecidable by ordinary Turing machines. In the positive direction, termination and correctness must hold for every finite input, with the stated rejection convention on invalid strings. In the negative direction, the proof must rule out every candidate total decider, not merely refute one proposed algorithm or one recursively specified axiom system. A computably equivalent precise syntax may be used if its effective correspondence with the encoding and sentence semantics is proved. A procedure that is correct whenever it terminates but lacks a universal termination proof does not meet the positive criterion. Deciding only a syntactic fragment qualifies only if the proof also establishes decidability of the full stated theory. Neither assuming Schanuel’s conjecture nor assuming another unresolved hypothesis is an unconditional resolution; the hypothesis would itself have to be proved in the accepted Lean development. Numerical evaluation with any fixed precision, bounded search for real solutions, or a time-complexity lower bound does not replace this exact decidability target.
cards.why: A central boundary in exact algorithmic reasoning over real numbers: polynomial real arithmetic is decidable, while adding one standard analytic function connects logical truth to unresolved transcendence questions. Its resolution would determine whether a uniform symbolic decision procedure can handle all finite first-order specifications involving real exponentiation, with consequences for verification problems already reducible to this theory.

context_blocks.text: Tarski’s decision theorem covers polynomial equations and inequalities over the reals with arbitrary first-order quantifiers. Adding the single function \(\exp\) asks whether that global decidability survives beyond polynomial arithmetic. The input remains a finite symbolic formula: a quantified real is part of the semantics, not a real number that must somehow be supplied as an infinite input string.

The target includes exact equalities and unrestricted quantifier alternation. For example, \(\forall x\,(x>0\Rightarrow\exists y\,\exp(y)=x)\) expresses surjectivity onto the positive reals; the implication here is an abbreviation for a disjunction in the specified syntax. Individual familiar identities are decidable, but they do not supply a machine for every sentence. Approximating an exponential value is also a different task: arbitrarily accurate approximations need not by themselves decide whether a given expression is exactly zero.

Wilkie proved model completeness of the real exponential theory in 1996: every formula is equivalent, in that theory, to an existential formula. The structure is also o-minimal, meaning that every definable subset of the real line is a finite union of points and intervals. These are strong finiteness properties, but neither statement alone certifies an algorithm for exact truth. The June 2026 paper recalls both results and distinguishes model completeness from completeness and effective axiomatization.

Macintyre and Wilkie proved decidability assuming the real form of Schanuel’s conjecture. That hypothesis says that whenever \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), the field \(\mathbb Q(a_1,\ldots,a_n,\exp(a_1),\ldots,\exp(a_n))\) has transcendence degree at least \(n\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Linear independence means that a rational linear combination is zero only when every coefficient is zero; transcendence degree is the maximum number of elements algebraically independent over \(\mathbb Q\), meaning that no nonzero rational polynomial in those elements vanishes. Wilkie’s 1997 exposition explicitly describes the decidability result as conditional. The stronger conjecture about complex tuples is not required for this real-theory implication.

The algorithmic survey distinguishes Schanuel’s transcendence conjecture from a weaker effective separation statement equivalent to decidability. For integer polynomials \(p,q_1,\ldots,q_n\) in \(2n\) variables, set \(F_p(x)=p(x_1,\ldots,x_n,\exp(x_1),\ldots,\exp(x_n))\), and define \(F_{q_i}\) similarly. The weak statement asks for a computable positive integer \(\eta\) such that every common zero \(\gamma\) of the \(F_{q_i}\) with invertible derivative matrix \((\partial F_{q_i}/\partial x_j)(\gamma)\) satisfies \(|F_p(\gamma)|\leq1/\eta\Rightarrow F_p(\gamma)=0\). The source explains that some such separation value exists; the unresolved requirement is its uniform computability. Consequently, failure of the stronger Schanuel conjecture would not by itself establish undecidability.

Berarducci and Gallinaro’s revision of 23 June 2026 gives a new axiomatization of the full real exponential theory under the real Schanuel hypothesis. Its unconditional theorem concerns model completeness for axioms of a restricted exponential function: this function equals \(\exp(x)\) on \((-1,1)\) and zero outside that interval. Completeness for their axiom systems, including the unrestricted exponential system, still uses the conjecture. Thus the unconditional theorem is not an unconditional decision procedure for the full language here.

One application comes from weighted automata assigning nonnegative rational values to finite words. The CONCUR 2020 source asks whether two initial states define functions \(f,g\) with \(f(w)\leq Cg(w)\) for every word \(w\) and some constant \(C>0\). The general problem is undecidable, but when both positive-weight languages are bounded—each contained in a product \(w_1^*\cdots w_k^*\) of repetitions of finitely many fixed words—the source reduces the comparison to real-exponential arithmetic and obtains conditional decidability. Decidability of this theory would make that application unconditional; the unrelated undecidability result for arbitrary automata does not refute this theory’s decidability.

cards.title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold \(r\in [0,1]\), decide whether \(v_{G}(s)>r\), where \(v_{G}(s)=\sup _{\sigma} \inf _{\tau} \Pr _{s}^{\sigma ,\tau}\)[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
cards.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
cards.why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

importance.reason: A canonical efficient decision problem combining adversarial control and randomness.

context_blocks.text: This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\). That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies \(x=(x+x)/2\) for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability \(2^{- k}\), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only \(O(k)\) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.

The exact branch formerly indexed as TCS-2427 asks for a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm returning optimal positional strategies for a finite, explicitly given, two-player zero-sum turn-based game. Each state is owned by one player; every available action has a rational reward to Max and a rational probability distribution over successor states. Min receives the opposite reward. A common rational discount multiplier \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) is part of the binary input, and Max's objective is \(\mathbb E[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r_t]\). Multiplication by \(1-\gamma\) leaves optimal strategies unchanged. The factor is constant during a play but may approach one across inputs. Time must be polynomial in the complete encoding length, including \(\gamma\); polynomial dependence on \(1/(1-\gamma)\) alone is insufficient. Exact solving of this class and simple stochastic games are polynomial-time equivalent. The source's additional approximation branch has no precision selected here.

The 2023 source explicitly separates the known constant-discount algorithms from the input-dependent discount question. The checked 2024 paper invokes the reduction of discounted game values and optimal policies to SSGs. These connections motivate consolidating the exact branch into the present threshold problem; they do not establish that its polynomial-time target is solved.

cards.title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
cards.formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
cards.definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.

context_blocks.text: Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type \(A_{0}\) of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, \(A_{1}\) gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—\(A_{2}\) gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the question distinguishes its externally specified \(D_{j}\) from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for \(D_{100}\) and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary \(n:\mathbb{N}\). The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this question asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over \(U_{0}\) preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
cards.why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

importance.reason: The defining question of whether efficient computation can be inherently sequential.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.

context_blocks.text: Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC.
The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.
