sentences: The question asks for globally learning well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures with both polynomial samples and polynomial computation.
The weights, centers and unequal component scales are hidden, and all must be recovered to the source’s stated relative accuracy up to one permutation.
The source’s efficient local refinement requires initialization that its sample-efficient procedure does not find in polynomial time.
Later algorithms improve separation or dimension dependence but retain assumptions or parameter costs that do not meet the full target.
A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform end-to-end learner under the explicit separation, access and arithmetic-cost conventions.

cards.definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.

source_formulation.text: At the well-separated spherical-Gaussian regime of the paper, can parameter learning from unlabeled samples use both polynomial time and polynomial sample complexity?
source_formulation.caption: Source paraphrase

context_blocks.text: Expectation maximization alternates between estimating component membership probabilities and updating parameters. The source proves strong local refinement guarantees and an information-theoretically sample-efficient initialization. The latter can be computationally expensive, which is why its final initialization discussion still asks for an end-to-end polynomial algorithm.

The source permits unknown unequal spherical variances and unequal weights. Its Theorem 9 measures mean error in units of each component’s standard deviation and asks for a smaller relative scale error as dimension grows. The completed statement preserves those parameter guarantees, rather than replacing them with a total-variation approximation or clustering-only task.

Li–Liu obtain polynomial-time learning for identity-covariance mixtures when separation is \(\Omega(\log^{1/2+c}k)\) for any fixed \(c>0\). Their parameter-estimation guarantee is a major improvement over earlier polynomial separation requirements. The theorem does not set \(c=0\), and its common known covariance differs from the full unequal-scale formulation.

Qiao and coauthors give a Fourier-based algorithm with stronger separation guarantees in the low-dimensional regime \(d=O(\log k/\log\log k)\). Their general runtime is polynomial in \(k\) multiplied by a function of dimension, separation and accuracy. This does not provide one polynomial bound over the full high-dimensional parameter range.

The 2026 sparse-Fourier method efficiently learns mixtures whose component characteristic functions decay sufficiently slowly. The main theorem explicitly excludes Gaussians. Its combined treatment of slow- and fast-decaying components retains separate separation and runtime dependencies for the latter, so it does not establish the present Gaussian threshold.

COLT 2026 gives substantial improvements for nonspherical centered mixtures and mixtures with identical unknown covariance. The centered result retains a nonpolynomial function of inverse minimum weight, and the equal-covariance result retains a weight-dependent exponent. Neither theorem supplies the fully polynomial growing-component guarantee specified here.

cards.formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to \{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
cards.why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.

cards.definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most \(n^{- d}\) for each integer \(d\ge 1\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

context_blocks.text: Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

Messages consist of one bit. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The question permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the corresponding key-agreement implication has a different conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this question.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The question therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this question.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The question therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.
cards.why: One-way functions are a basic foundation for computational pseudorandomness and cryptography. This question asks whether a worst-case separation between decision and verification already forces a function whose efficiently generated outputs resist inversion on average, without a separate cryptographic assumption.

importance.reason: Connects worst-case verification hardness to average-case cryptographic security.

context_blocks.text: Existence of one-way functions implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The converse asks for much more than a function with occasional difficult inputs: the security experiment generates inputs uniformly, and every efficient inverter must have negligible overall success at all sufficiently large lengths. Worst-case inversion difficulty by itself does not give that distributional guarantee.

Average-case decision hardness and one-wayness have distinct requirements. The former can concern a language paired with a chosen feasible instance distribution. Here instances are images of uniform inputs under the same efficiently computable function whose inversion is tested. The adversary may exploit collisions and only needs to find any permitted preimage; hard reconstruction of the original sampled input is not enough.

Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish that one-way functions suffice for cryptographic pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. A cryptographic generator efficiently expands uniform random bits so that polynomial-time statistical tests cannot distinguish its outputs from uniform strings with nonnegligible advantage. This explains the broad consequences of the primitive without adding encryption, a trapdoor or injectivity to this question.

Known nonadaptive oracle-reduction barriers show that certain reductions from NP-complete worst-case problems to average inversion would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such reductions choose all their oracle questions before receiving answers and must work for every oracle satisfying the average-success promise. The barrier concerns that reduction class; it does not establish the negation of the unrestricted implication.

Liu–Pass give an unconditional equivalence between one-way functions and a particular boundary-hardness condition for randomized time-bounded description complexity. Their corresponding statement for deterministic description complexity uses an exponential circuit-hardness assumption. An equivalence with a specialized hardness condition does not by itself establish that condition from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); the inspected paper explicitly retains this missing connection.

The April 2026 Liu–Mazor–Pass paper derives conditional pseudorandom generators and restricted zero-knowledge consequences from hardness of specific gap-description problems. A conditional generator’s seed distribution may be inefficient to sample, whereas an ordinary cryptographic generator uses uniform seeds. The paper retains additional hardness hypotheses and says that obtaining ordinary one-way functions from plain worst-case gap hardness remains beyond its results.

The eventual security requirement matters to both sides of the question. To disprove one-wayness of a candidate, a fixed inverter with noticeable success at arbitrarily large lengths is enough. To prove one-wayness, security on a sparse infinite subsequence is insufficient. The requested implication therefore cannot be replaced by an infinitely-often variant without changing the target.

cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal:
Does ordinary polynomial-hard decisional Learning With Errors imply indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, circular-security or leakage-resilience hypothesis?

Precisely, let \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) be the fixed classical nonuniform decisional-LWE assumption below, with prime modulus \(q(n)\ge n^4\) and Gaussian width \(n\). Let \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) assert the existence of the uniform classical probabilistic obfuscator defined below, with security against all classical polynomial-size circuit families. The proposition to establish or refute is the implication
\[H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\ \Longrightarrow\ I_{\mathrm{circ}}.\]
All modulus, error, sample, correctness and security quantifiers are fixed in the definitions. Neither subexponential hardness nor additional information supplied about the LWE secret or errors is part of the premise.
cards.definitions:
LWE assumption. For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(q(n)\) be the least prime at least \(n^4\), and let \(\mathbb Z_q\) mean integers modulo \(q=q(n)\). Define the probability distribution \(\chi_n\) on the integers by
\[\Pr_{e\leftarrow\chi_n}[e=t]=\frac{\exp(-\pi t^2/n^2)}{\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\exp(-\pi j^2/n^2)}\quad(t\in\mathbb Z).\]
The positive normalizing sum converges. This specifies an exact mathematical distribution; it is not an input consisting of real-number samples or a unit-cost real-arithmetic oracle.

For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(m=m(n)\), compare the following distributions:
\[X_n=(A,As+e\bmod q),\qquad Y_n=(A,u),\]
where \(A\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times n}\), \(s\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^n\), the \(m\) entries of \(e\) are independent samples of \(\chi_n\), and \(u\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). All these choices are mutually independent before forming \(As+e\); the same secret \(s\) is used in every row. Reduce each integer error modulo \(q\). Each residue is encoded as its canonical representative in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), using \(\lceil\log_2q\rceil\) bits, and the matrix and vector are fully listed. Public parameters \(n,m,q\) accompany the encoding. No leakage or other secret-dependent hint is given.

An ensemble pair is computationally indistinguishable if, for every family \((D_n)\) of classical Boolean circuits with description length bounded by some polynomial in \(n\),
\[\left|\Pr[D_n(X_n)=1]-\Pr[D_n(Y_n)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(n\). A nonnegative function \(\nu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), there is \(n_0\) such that \(\nu(n)\le n^{-c}\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). Circuit families need not be uniformly computable and may hardwire polynomially many advice bits. Deterministic distinguishers suffice here; private random coins can equivalently be allowed. The assertion \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) is indistinguishability for every such sample count and every such distinguisher family. This is asymptotic polynomial security, not a bound on the cost of attacks at a single numerical parameter.

Circuit model. A circuit has \(a\ge0\) labelled input bits, \(g\ge0\) gates in topological order, and \(b\ge1\) designated output wires. Gates are binary AND or OR, unary NOT, or constants 0 and 1. Wires may be reused. Gate predecessors must be inputs or earlier gates; each output names an existing input or gate. This defines a total deterministic function \(C:\{0,1\}^a\to\{0,1\}^b\). Constant gates are allowed as part of the conventional Boolean basis.

Use the explicit encoding \(1^a0\), then length-delimited counts \(U(g),U(b)\), followed by every gate and every output index. Here \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\). Each gate has a fixed three-bit type tag and the appropriate zero, one or two \(U\)-encoded predecessor indices. Input nodes come first, then gate nodes; unused tags and out-of-range indices are invalid. Each output is a \(U\)-encoded index, and trailing bits are forbidden. Define \(|C|\) to be the total description length. Thus every input, gate and output is explicitly counted; exponentially many undeclared inputs or succinctly generated gate lists are not allowed. Two circuits are equivalent when their input/output arities coincide and their outputs agree on every input, exactly.

Obfuscator. There is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(O\) and positive integers \(K,d\). On \((1^\lambda,C)\), for every integer \(\lambda\ge2\), it halts within \(K(\lambda+|C|+1)^d\) bit steps on every sequence of independent fair random bits. On a valid circuit it always returns a valid circuit with the same input/output arities, of description length at most the same polynomial bound. Malformed descriptions may be rejected, within the clock. All input reading, randomness, arithmetic and output writing are charged. There is no advice, quantum state, oracle, trusted setup or free preprocessing.

Functionality requires a uniform error bound over all circuits at each size scale. For every positive integer polynomial bound \(p\), there exists a negligible function \(\mu_p\) such that for every \(\lambda\ge2\) and valid \(|C|\le p(\lambda)\),
\[\Pr_r[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^a:\ O(1^\lambda,C;r)(x)=C(x)]\ge1-\mu_p(\lambda).\]
One successful output must be correct on all inputs simultaneously; a separate high success probability for each input is insufficient.

Indistinguishability requires that for every pair of circuit sequences \((C_{0,\lambda},C_{1,\lambda})\) of polynomially bounded description length, with equal description lengths, matching arities and equivalent functions for each \(\lambda\), and every classical polynomial-size distinguisher family \((D_\lambda)\), the advantage
\[\left|\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{0,\lambda};r))=1]-\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{1,\lambda};r))=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). The sequences themselves need not be efficiently generated. Distinguishers can hardwire the circuit pair and arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information. Variable-length outputs are presented with their length and zero padding to a common polynomial bound determined by the pair's size bound and the clock; actual length remains visible. Probabilities use fresh independent obfuscator coins. No efficiently verifiable certificate of circuit equivalence is supplied or required. The assertion \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) is existence of one machine and clock meeting both functionality and security for every polynomial size scale.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\Rightarrow I_{\mathrm{circ}}\), or of its full logical negation. A positive construction must prove the stated uniform efficiency, simultaneous all-input functionality, and security against all nonuniform polynomial-size classical distinguishers using only the specified LWE premise and proved mathematical facts. Any parameter changes used inside a construction must be justified from that premise. The literal negation is \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\land\neg I_{\mathrm{circ}}\). Refuting one candidate, excluding only black-box reductions, or separating the notions in an oracle world does not establish this unrelativized negation. A construction needing stronger quantitative hardness, circular security or auxiliary-leakage resilience does not prove the specified implication unless those properties are themselves derived from the fixed premise.
cards.why: General indistinguishability obfuscation supports cryptographic capabilities well beyond ordinary encryption. Deriving it from one standard noisy-linear-equation assumption would connect that broad power to a much simpler foundation. The precise quantitative premise matters: an implication from stronger security or from secret-dependent hints does not determine the power of ordinary polynomial-hard LWE.

The February 2026 JACM theorem uses four assumptions and stronger quantitative security; circular, CRO and Equivocal-LWE proposals add premises. The April/June 2026 general candidate is explicitly heuristic, and the September copy-protection application assumes iO. context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of the same function. It requires their obfuscations to be computationally indistinguishable when the original descriptions have equal size. It does not promise that a function hides information already revealed by its outputs, nor does it equate functionally different programs. These distinctions separate the mathematical notion from an informal claim that code is unreadable.

Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement: whatever can be learned from the code should be reproducible from oracle access to the function. Their revised full paper explicitly introduces the weaker indistinguishability comparison. Its impossibility result therefore does not supply a negative answer to this question.

LWE describes noisy linear equations over a finite residue field. The same hidden vector is used in all rows, while fresh independent errors perturb the products. Regev connects suitable LWE distributions to worst-case lattice problems by a quantum reduction. That historical foundation is evidence for studying LWE, not a proof of the exact classical nonuniform hardness hypothesis selected here. In particular, its rounded-Gaussian notation should not be silently identified with the integer-Gaussian convention.

Jain, Lin and Sahai construct iO using four well-studied assumptions. The February 2026 journal theorem lists LWE, sparse-noise LPN over large prime fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and DLIN in bilinear groups. It requires subexponential security guarantees and a subexponential LWE modulus-to-noise ratio. Both the extra assumptions and the quantitative regime exceed the premise here. The journal publication follows earlier work; it is not a new LWE-only construction.

Their follow-up removes LWE from the sufficient set, leaving the other three assumptions. Its introduction explicitly raises the possibility that LWE alone might suffice. Removing one assumption from a conjunction does not show that the removed assumption implies the conclusion. The distinction between subexponential security for its iO theorem and polynomial security for its functional-encryption consequence also remains substantive.

The circular-security construction eliminates factoring and pairing assumptions, but its theorem still assumes subexponential LWE hardness together with a key-randomness circular form of shielded randomness-leakage security. The latter experiment provides structured information involving encryption keys and ciphertext randomness. Its Definition 7 is an additional security premise; plain noisy LWE samples do not contain these hints. The paper also repairs a gap in an earlier efficiency transformation.

Later lattice proposals continue to separate ordinary LWE from strengthened assumptions. Hsieh, Jain and Lin explicitly introduce Circular Security with Random Opening, an LWE-with-hints assumption. Their abstract discusses attacks on earlier hint assumptions and presents the new proposal as a different target for cryptanalysis. No reduction from the ordinary LWE premise is asserted in the inspected abstract.

Cini, Lai and Woo instead use NTRU and a new Equivocal LWE assumption alongside other lattice assumptions. Their abstract qualifies the post-quantum construction and identifies possible cryptanalytic targets. A construction based on lattice assumptions can be an important advance without establishing that plain LWE alone suffices.

The April 2026 authentication preprint, revised in June, likewise distinguishes several claims. Its lattice tool assumes decomposed LWE; its pseudorandom-obfuscation result additionally assumes subexponentially secure iO. A separate general-iO proposal is expressly labelled heuristic. Neither the extra-premise theorem nor that heuristic is a proof of the implication posed here.

The September 2026 trapdoor-function preprint assumes both iO and LWE for copy protection. Its separate LWE-only key-leasing result concerns another primitive. This recent application uses general iO as an input assumption rather than deriving it, so it does not close the source question.

original.text: The source asks broadly whether LWE alone suffices for general iO. This card retains the explicit editorial variant selected on 10 September: least-prime modulus at least n^4, integer Gaussian width n, polynomial sample counts, ordinary negligible-advantage security against classical nonuniform polynomial-size circuits, and a uniform classical obfuscator with negligible probability of any functionality error. These exact parameters are a formulation choice, not parameters asserted by the source. The yes/no target is the mathematical implication itself, not a claim that every black-box construction exists or a task to prove LWE hardness. Importance remains 97.

cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal:
In the classical plain model, does the existence of public-key encryption secure against chosen-plaintext attacks imply the existence of 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party?

Let \(E\) assert the existence of the bit-encryption scheme defined below, and let \(T\) assert the existence of the two-party protocol and simulators defined below. The target is the unrelativized implication
\[E\ \Longrightarrow\ T.\]
All honest algorithms and simulators are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical machines; security is against arbitrary nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. The implication may use the full code of the encryption algorithms, non-black-box reasoning and polynomially many messages. It must not assume an additional property of encryption unless that property is proved to follow from the stated premise.
cards.definitions:
Common conventions. The security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\) is provided as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). A nonnegative function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), some \(\lambda_0\) satisfies \(\mu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\) for all \(\lambda\ge\lambda_0\). An algorithm is uniform probabilistic polynomial time if it has one fixed finite multitape Turing-machine program and a bound \(K(L+1)^d\) on its bit steps for every input of total length \(L\) and every sequence of independent fair random bits, for some fixed positive integers \(K,d\). Reading, arithmetic, coin generation and all output bits are charged. Malformed inputs may be rejected but must satisfy the clock. There is no advice, ideal oracle, quantum resource or uncharged preprocessing.

For polynomial-length random bit strings \(X_\lambda,Y_\lambda\), write \(X_\lambda\approx_c Y_\lambda\) when for every Boolean circuit family \((D_\lambda)\) of polynomially bounded description length,
\[\left|\Pr[D_\lambda(X_\lambda)=1]-\Pr[D_\lambda(Y_\lambda)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Such a family need not be uniformly generated. It may hardwire polynomial-length auxiliary information, including the input sequence under consideration. Deterministic circuits with binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants suffice; private random coins could equivalently be allowed. Encodings expose actual string lengths, with zero padding to a common polynomial bound for the distinguisher. Tuples and messages are encoded by their number of components and each component's length followed by its bits. Nonnegative lengths use \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\).

Public-key encryption. A scheme consists of three uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms, with public code:
\[(pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\quad z\leftarrow\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m),\quad \widehat m\leftarrow\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,z).\]
Keys and ciphertexts are ordinary finite bit strings; \(m\in\{0,1\}\), and decryption returns a bit or a failure symbol \(\bot\). All invocations use fresh independent coins. Keys generated at parameter \(\lambda\), honest ciphertexts and their encodings have polynomial length in \(\lambda\). Correctness requires one negligible function \(\mu_E\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and both message bits,
\[\Pr[\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m))\ne m]\le\mu_E(\lambda),\]
where the probability includes fresh key-generation, encryption and any decryption randomness.

IND-CPA security for bits means
\[(pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,0))\ \approx_c\ (pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,1)),\]
with fresh keys and encryption coins in each experiment. The secret key is not given to the distinguisher. The encryption algorithm is public, so polynomially many encryptions chosen by an attacker can be computed locally. No decryption oracle is available. For this bit-message case the two displayed challenge distributions specify the chosen-plaintext confidentiality requirement. The assertion \(E\) is existence of any scheme satisfying this correctness and security, without algebraic, rerandomization, key-sampling or ciphertext-sampling promises.

Oblivious transfer. The sender \(S\) receives private bits \((m_0,m_1)\), and the receiver \(R\) receives a private choice bit \(c\). Both receive \(1^\lambda\), have independent private fair coins, and exchange a finite ordered sequence of classical messages directly. There is one fixed protocol, with polynomially many bit steps per party, messages and communicated bits on every honest execution and every random-tape choice. Equivalently, all these quantities are bounded by some \(B(\lambda)=K(\lambda+1)^d\) independent of the inputs. The receiver outputs \(y\in\{0,1,\bot\}\); the sender has no output. Correctness requires a negligible \(\mu_T\) such that
\[\forall\lambda\ \forall(m_0,m_1,c)\in\{0,1\}^3:\quad\Pr[y=m_c]\ge1-\mu_T(\lambda).\]
The failure symbol counts as an error. There is no requirement of two rounds or constant rounds.

Static semi-honest corruption means that at most one party is designated corrupted before execution, then follows the prescribed algorithm with the prescribed coin distribution while retaining all information it sees. It may afterwards apply any polynomial-size computation to this information. It does not modify messages, bias its randomness, change its input during the protocol or erase data to satisfy a security condition. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_S\) includes the sender's input, its complete random tape and all sent/received messages. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_R\) includes the receiver's input, its complete random tape, all messages and its final output. A fixed polynomial number of fair bits may be sampled at the start and unused bits retained. Internal computation is determined by the input, coins and messages and is thus recoverable from the view.

Privacy requires two fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(\operatorname{Sim}_S,\operatorname{Sim}_R\). For every sequence of input triples \((m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\), the following ensemble pairs must be computationally indistinguishable:
\[\operatorname{View}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda}),\]
\[\operatorname{View}_R(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_R(1^\lambda,c_\lambda,m_{c_\lambda,\lambda}).\]
The source of randomness on the left is an honest interaction of both parties; each right-hand experiment uses the simulator's own fresh coins. Input sequences need not be efficiently computable. The sender simulator receives no choice bit; the receiver simulator receives no unchosen message. The simulators precede the quantifiers over sequences and distinguishers, and have worst-case polynomial clocks rather than merely expected polynomial time. The assertion \(T\) is existence of a protocol and simulators satisfying these requirements.

The plain model supplies no common reference string, random oracle, trusted third party or hardware, and no pre-shared correlated randomness or secret. It permits only the independent randomness and communication just described. The security task is one standalone execution with static passive corruption; malicious deviation, adaptive corruption, fairness, guaranteed delivery against abort and universal composability are not additional requirements.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(E\Rightarrow T\) or its full logical negation. A positive proof must obtain the specified uniform protocol and simulators, establish all polynomial clocks and communication bounds, and prove correctness and both privacy ensembles from the encryption premise alone. Non-black-box use of encryption code and non-black-box security arguments are permitted. The literal negative answer is \(E\land\neg T\) in the ordinary, unrelativized model. An oracle world with encryption but no OT, a lower bound on black-box reductions, an attack on one protocol or a failure at a prescribed round count does not prove that negation. Any extra sampling or rerandomization property used by a proposed construction must also be derived from the premise.
cards.why: Public-key encryption protects a message from someone without its decryption key. Oblivious transfer must also protect a sender from a receiver who is entitled to learn one selected message, while hiding that selection from the sender. Determining whether the first capability already implies the second would clarify a basic boundary between secure communication and general private computation.

importance.reason: Tests whether secure communication already supports general private computation.

A fully black-box compiler establishes the strength of semi-honest OT by deriving malicious OT and general secure computation in the stated standalone model.
A further black-box barrier concerns optimal fair coin tossing from PKE or key agreement.
OT is constructed from encryption with the additional public rerandomization property.
The Minicrypt preprint distinguishes non-black-box OT from standard-model interactive hash functions from their random-oracle construction.
The updatable-encryption journal article derives OT with specified extra oblivious-sampling properties.
A stabilizer-decoding hardness premise is claimed to support both classical PKE and OT, without a generic PKE-to-OT theorem.

context_blocks.text: The two privacy obligations are different. The sender must not learn the receiver’s choice, and the receiver must not learn anything about the unselected message beyond what its allowed input and output already imply. Simulation expresses both requirements without assuming the messages themselves are random or secret from all prior information. Correctness is separate: a protocol that exchanges nothing may reveal nothing, but it does not deliver the selected bit.

Gertner and coauthors ask directly whether public-key encryption implies OT. Their positive results require additional oblivious-sampling properties of public keys or ciphertexts. Their negative result constructs an oracle relative to which encryption exists but even semi-honest OT does not. That theorem is a substantial restriction on relativizing construction methods; it is not an ordinary-world separation of the two existence statements.

The historical oracle theorem also has an explicit uniformity qualification. Its authors prove security and separation for probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries and state that extension to nonuniform circuit adversaries would require further work. The security requirement permits nonuniform distinguishers, so the original theorem should not be presented as an exact separation for every quantifier in its definitions.

Allowing non-black-box techniques means a proof may use the actual finite descriptions of encryption algorithms. Replacing those algorithms by a freely chosen oracle can remove information that such a proof uses. An oracle barrier therefore cannot simply be reinterpreted as the negation of the unrestricted implication. The target also allows polynomially many rounds, so a barrier at a fixed small round count is insufficient.

Even passive-security OT is a powerful goal. Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box transformation from semi-honest OT to maliciously secure OT and then to general secure computation. Their formulation uses static corruption, standalone security and, for the stronger malicious task, simulators that may run in expected polynomial time. It does not promise fairness or delivery despite malicious abort. These are consequences in a specified model, not extra requirements silently added to this question.

Li, Zhang and Lin replace earlier oblivious-sampling conditions by public rerandomizability: given a public key, an algorithm can turn a ciphertext into a fresh one with the same plaintext. Their abstract gives OT constructions under this property. IND-CPA confidentiality by itself does not include such an algorithm, so the result covers an enriched encryption primitive.

The March 2026 updatable-encryption article likewise retains precise extra properties. Its two-round OT implication uses oblivious samplability of original ciphertexts and update tokens; its three-round implication uses oblivious samplability of updated ciphertexts. Updatable encryption is a structured symmetric encryption primitive with tokens for transforming ciphertexts across keys. The inspected theorem summaries do not start from an arbitrary IND-CPA public-key scheme.

The January 2026 Minicrypt preprint gives a particularly relevant distinction between a non-black-box implication and an oracle construction. Its abstract claims OT from a standard-model oblivious interactive hash function, and separately constructs that hash primitive in a random-oracle model. It explicitly says that these two statements cannot be composed into OT from a random oracle: the non-black-box step applies only to an ordinary finite implementation. No generic construction of that implementation from arbitrary PKE is claimed in the checked abstract.

The March 2026 stabilizer-decoding preprint gives another kind of progress: a new average-case hardness premise supports both PKE and OT. Having a common sufficient assumption does not show that either primitive follows from every implementation of the other. The additional algebraic structure of that decoding problem remains part of its construction’s foundation.

Fair coin tossing provides a related comparison. Maji and Wang prove limits on protocols that use PKE or key agreement as black boxes, whereas an OT resource supports the optimal fairness scale considered there. That result concerns a different functionality and a restricted construction model. It adds evidence about the hierarchy without resolving the unrestricted semi-honest OT implication.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
cards.why: This asks whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable total problems beyond classical randomization. It identifies the exact classical lower bound needed to turn an efficient quantum decision algorithm into an unconditional separation of computational power.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states strict total-language containment as Conjecture 11.5. Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. Bounded searches located no full matching unrelativized separation or equality claim. An unverified claim that P differs from both BPP and BQP does not decide this comparison. This review checks statement and source scope; it does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all subsequent literature.

context_blocks.text: Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes here still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.

cards.context:
Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes here still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\).
cards.why: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation.
