context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally reversible: either endpoint label fixes exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Despite this simplicity, the conjecture asks whether an almost perfectly consistent collection is NP-hard to distinguish from one for which every labeling violates almost all constraints. This is a promise decision gap, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum.

For example, with two labels an identity permutation asks for equal labels, while a transposition asks for different labels. Three transposition constraints on the edges of a triangle have value \(2/3\). This illustrates how individually consistent requirements can conflict globally; the conjecture quantifies over larger alphabets and much more extreme gaps.

Exact satisfiability, meaning \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\), is polynomial-time decidable in this explicit model. The positive completeness error \(\varepsilon\) is therefore an essential feature of the conjecture. A uniformly random labeling satisfies an expected fraction \(1/q\) of the edges, so every instance has value at least \(1/q\). In particular, if \(\delta<1/q\), there are no NO instances. The alphabet cannot be fixed in advance of all soundness thresholds.

Raghavendra’s 2008 theorem ties Unique-Games-based hardness to a general semidefinite-programming framework for constraint satisfaction over a fixed finite domain. Under UGC, its approximation guarantees are optimal up to arbitrary fixed accuracy, with the usual consequence for polynomial-time algorithms requiring a complexity separation. This explains why one apparently narrow family of permutation constraints governs many approximation thresholds.

Arora, Barak and Steurer’s 2010 theorem gives, for an absolute \(\alpha>0\), an \(\exp(qn^{\varepsilon^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm returning a \((1-\varepsilon^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling on an \(n\)-vertex, \((1-\varepsilon)\)-satisfiable instance. For fixed \(q\) and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\), this is subexponential but does not give polynomial time. Its dependence on completeness is compatible with reductions whose polynomial exponent depends on the desired gap.

The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies that, for every fixed positive soundness threshold, Unique Games is NP-hard with completeness \(1/2\). Khot’s exposition states this as Theorem 2.20. The conclusion leaves the near-one completeness in UGC unresolved. The 2025 journal publication of one part of the proof sequence records the historical role of its conditional intermediate theorem and still states full UGC separately as Conjecture 1.4.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims the \(4\)-to-\(1\) Games Conjecture with perfect completeness. Its constraints are projections in which each right-hand label has four preimages, rather than bijections. Theorem 1.6 is a major related hardness claim, with graph-coloring consequences, but does not prove the permutation-constraint UGC. The same introduction retains UGC as Conjecture 1.4 and identifies completeness \(1/2\) as the existing Unique Games hardness frontier. Its full proof has not been independently verified.

Yoshida’s May 2026 tolerant-testing preprint concerns adjacency-list queries and distinguishes small from larger optimum violation fractions. Its Theorem 1.1 requires \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\), where \(\rho\) is the larger violation threshold and \(c_q>0\) depends on the fixed alphabet. For the UGC gap, \(\rho=1-\delta\); the displayed assumption does not hold for every input size when the positive errors and alphabet are fixed. Thus the tester’s sublinear query bound does not refute this fixed-parameter, all-instance hardness statement.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Does Densest \(k\)-Subgraph have a deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation on all explicitly given finite simple undirected unweighted graphs?

For \(n\ge1\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If \(G=([n],E)\) and \(1\le k\le n\), define
\[e_G(S)=|\{\{u,v\}\in E:u,v\in S\}|,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max_{\substack{T\subseteq[n]\\|T|=k}}e_G(T).\]
The proposition is that there exist one real constant \(C\ge1\), positive integer constants \(D,d\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) such that, on every encoded input of length \(L\), \(A\) halts within \(D(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and on every valid \((G,k)\) it outputs an explicitly represented set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfying
\[|S|=k\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\,e_G(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(G,k).\]
The same algorithm, constants and polynomial clock must work for all \(n,G,k\).
cards.definitions:
The graph has exactly the labelled vertices \([n]\), including isolated vertices. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, with no repetitions, loops, weights or directions. Its input is \(U(n)U(k)\) followed by the \(n(n-1)/2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of pairs \((u,v)\) with \(u<v\). Here \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is the canonical binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(a\), \(\ell=|b|\), and zero uses \(b=0\). The code must have precisely the indicated number of adjacency bits, with \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le n\). Invalid encodings may be rejected; the clock applies to them too. This dense explicit encoding is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. A succinct circuit or edge oracle is not an input representation .

The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. A one at position \(i\) means vertex \(i\) belongs to \(S\), and exactly \(k\) bits must be one. The objective counts each internal edge once. The maximum exists because the family of \(k\)-subsets is finite and nonempty. An estimate of the optimum without an accompanying vertex set does not satisfy the output requirement.

Running time counts ordinary bounded-symbol Turing-machine steps, including reading input, arithmetic and writing all output bits. The machine has one fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of tapes. The constants cannot depend on graph size, \(k\), edge density or any promise about the input. No advice, randomness, quantum operations or uncharged oracle is supplied. A running time whose polynomial exponent increases with \(k\) does not meet the clock.

The approximation is purely multiplicative and holds on every valid input, with no additive loss, input-distribution exception or probability of failure. When \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=0\), the inequality is automatic but the output must still be a valid \(k\)-set. This includes \(k=1\), edgeless graphs and \(n=1\). The case \(k=n\) is included. The quantifier over \(C\) could equivalently use a positive integer, since rounding an admissible real factor upward preserves the guarantee.

Exactly \(k\) vertices is part of the target. On these feasible sets, maximizing internal edge count, average degree \(2e_G(S)/k\), or edges per vertex \(e_G(S)/k\) gives the same approximation ratio. If the number of selected vertices is allowed to vary, these objectives are no longer interchangeable. A guarantee for at least \(k\) vertices, a special graph class, a planted input distribution or a randomized algorithm is a different statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this proposition or of its full logical negation. A positive answer must specify one deterministic algorithm and universal constants, prove the global polynomial clock, and prove both exact output cardinality and the approximation inequality on every valid graph and parameter. A negative answer must exclude every such constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm. Equivalently, for every deterministic polynomial-time machine that always outputs a valid \(k\)-set and every fixed \(C\ge1\), some valid input must satisfy \(C e_G(A(G,k))<\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)\). A lower bound conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis, or a limitation of a specified relaxation or algorithm family, does not by itself prove the full negation.
cards.why: Densest k-Subgraph asks whether a prescribed number of vertices can capture a constant fraction of the greatest possible internal connectivity. Its approximation landscape is a central gap between available algorithms, conditional hardness and what follows from the usual P-versus-NP assumption. The answer also matters for several graph optimization objectives linked to its approximability.

importance.reason: A defining gap between approximation algorithms and established hardness foundations.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The deterministic constant-factor question remains source-open in the inspected literature. ETH conditionally excludes such an algorithm, but is unproved; the May 2026 primary source explicitly retains the missing NP-hardness of even 1.001 approximation under the usual P≠NP framework. The March exact-penalty result and August unrestricted/at-least-k density preprint do not claim the specified exactly-k guarantee. The bounded later-work check is not an independent certification of every cited proof or an exhaustive absence-of-results claim.

context_blocks.text: The exact cardinality makes the objective distinctive. A large region of moderate density can be an excellent answer when size is unrestricted or only bounded below, yet it need not contain a k-vertex region with a comparable fraction of the optimum for exactly k. The question asks for the actual selected vertices, so evaluating a continuous objective or estimating an optimum is insufficient.

Bhaskara and coauthors give an \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}\) time for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Their paper includes a deterministic combinatorial algorithm. Its title’s \(O(n^{1/4})\) endpoint requires quasipolynomial \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time in that analysis. The 2026 AAAI paper still describes the quarter-power-plus-epsilon bound as the general polynomial-time benchmark; neither bound is a universal constant.

Manurangsi proves that the Exponential Time Hypothesis rules out polynomial-time approximation within \(n^{1/(\log\log n)^c}\) for some universal \(c>0\). The paper states ETH as the absence of a deterministic \(2^{o(m)}\)-time algorithm for 3SAT with \(m\) clauses. Its hard YES instances contain a \(k\)-clique, a property called perfect completeness. The result already excludes every fixed approximation constant if ETH holds, but ETH is an unproved assumption stronger than \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

The corresponding conclusion under only P≠NP remains a different issue. The May 2026 at-least-k paper explicitly says that even NP-hardness of a 1.001 approximation for Densest k-Subgraph is not known. This is consistent with the ETH lower bound: different hypotheses support different conclusions. A proof of conditional hardness is significant evidence, but does not establish the unconditional negative answer required by the question.

Chuzhoy and coauthors propose a Low-Degree CSP conjecture. Together with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), it would exclude a polynomial-time \(2^{(\log n)^\varepsilon}\)-approximation for some \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\). Their stated consequence uses Cook-type reductions, which may make multiple oracle queries. The work also connects graph partitioning, dense coloring and other graph objectives, sometimes with quasipolynomial reductions. These are qualified conditional relationships rather than constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences.

The 2012 integrality gaps demonstrate limitations of specified strong semidefinite relaxations. They exhibit a separation between what a relaxation permits and the objective attained by genuine selected vertices. Such a separation constrains approximation arguments based on that relaxation; it does not rule out every polynomial-time algorithm.

Jones and coauthors give further Sum-of-Squares lower bounds in a planted-subgraph distinction model for \(k\le\sqrt n\). Under a sufficient penalty, its global optima correspond to the combinatorial problem, with an additional local-optimum correspondence. They are relevant recent progress, but neither is a claimed resolution of its constant-factor question.

cards.title: Matroid secretary conjecture
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), there is a randomized online selection strategy \(\mathcal A_M\) satisfying
\[\forall w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0},\qquad
\mathbb E_{\pi,U}\!\left[\sum_{e\in S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)}w(e)\right]
\ge\frac1C\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e)?\]
The element weights are fixed adversarially before a uniformly random arrival permutation \(\pi\) and the strategy's independent randomness \(U\) are chosen. Each acceptance decision is irrevocable and must preserve independence. The same \(C\) must work for all matroids and all weights.
cards.definitions:
A finite matroid consists of a finite ground set \(E\) and a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) of independent sets with two properties. First, \(B\subseteq A\in\mathcal I\) implies \(B\in\mathcal I\). Second, if \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(e\in B\setminus A\) satisfies \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). In particular, \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\). Loops, zero weights, ties and the empty ground set are allowed. The matroid rank is \(\max_{I\in\mathcal I}|I|\).

The strategy knows \(E\) and \(\mathcal I\) in advance, including all element identities and \(n=|E|\), but has no information about the weights of unarrived elements. At step \(t\), it sees the identity \(\pi(t)\) and its finite real weight \(w(\pi(t))\). Before the next arrival, it chooses to accept or reject that element. Its decision may use only the known matroid, the revealed prefix, its previous decisions and its random seed. An accepted element cannot subsequently be discarded, and a rejected element cannot subsequently be accepted. Every accepted prefix must belong to \(\mathcal I\), for every input, arrival order and seed. The notation \(S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)\) denotes the final accepted set.

A randomized strategy is a measurable nonanticipating decision rule; one may model its private randomness by \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\), independent of \(\pi\). The permutation is uniform among the \(n!\) permutations of \(E\) and independent of the fixed weight assignment. Expectations include these two sources of randomness. For every fixed assignment the optimum is finite, so the expected reward is well-defined and finite. If all feasible weights are zero, the inequality still applies with a zero right-hand side.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C\;\forall M\;\exists\mathcal A_M\;\forall w\). A strategy cannot be selected after seeing the weight assignment. The guarantee has no additive loss, no dependence of \(C\) on size or rank, and no high-probability requirement beyond the stated expectation. There is no restriction on computation, preprocessing or independence queries. This is the competitive-existence question in the known-matroid model, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights; no finite encoding or polynomial running time is appended.

context_blocks.text: The classical secretary task chooses one item whose unknown value is revealed on arrival. Matroids extend the feasibility rule to collections of items. For example, a uniform matroid permits any set up to a prescribed size, while a graphic matroid permits sets of edges containing no cycle. The offline optimum knows every weight; the online strategy sees only a random prefix at each decision.

Random arrival order and random assignment of weights are distinct sources of information. In the random-assignment variant, a multiset of weights is distributed uniformly among ground-set elements. Santiago, Sergeev and Zenklusen obtain a constant guarantee for that variant even without advance knowledge of the matroid. Their May 2023 preprint explicitly leaves the adversarial-assignment conjecture open. Its theorem cannot by itself justify the general claim here.

Before the new September claim, the cited general guarantee was \(O(\log\log r)\), with the small-rank cases treated separately, where \(r\) is the matroid rank. A growing rank-dependent factor differs from a universal constant, even though many particular matroid classes already admit constant guarantees.

Dughmi proves that a competitive secretary algorithm implies random-order contention resolution for arbitrarily correlated active sets, losing only the same multiplicative factor relative to the best offline guarantee. The later equivalence theorem establishes the converse at the level of universal constants. This connection concerns a known probability distribution and an information-theoretic guarantee; it does not require the distribution to be a product law.

Singla's preprint submitted on 13 September 2026 states in Theorem 3.1 that each element of a canonical offline optimum is accepted with probability at least \(1/4\), while the selected set is always independent. This would imply the displayed target with \(C=4\). The stated theorem allows fixed nonnegative values and needs only the ground-set size and independence queries on already arrived elements. Those assumptions are compatible with, and more restrictive than, the advance matroid knowledge.

The fresh preprint is recorded as a matching solution claim, pending independent verification. Its full PDF and theorem scope were inspected, but this review does not certify the complete proof. Section 4 separately announces extensions and defers their detailed proofs; those announcements are not treated as already established results. The paper also distinguishes the original constant-factor conjecture from the stronger proposed factor \(e\), where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm.

cards.why: This is a central question about the power of random arrival order in online selection under general independence constraints. A universal bound would apply across all matroids and is equivalent, through established reductions, to a general random-order contention-resolution guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed constant-competitiveness proposition, or of its full logical negation. A positive proof must give a finite universal constant and admissible strategies with the expected guarantee for every matroid and weight assignment. A negative proof must show that for every proposed finite constant some matroid defeats every admissible strategy on some fixed nonnegative weight assignment. A result for a restricted matroid family, randomly assigned weights, or a constant depending on rank does not settle this target. A newly posted proof claim is not itself a Lean-checked answer.

cards.title: Breaking two for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid instance \(I\) of the scheduling problem defined below, \(A\) outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) within \(K(L(I)+2)^d\) bit steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\]
Here \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial bound must work for every job count, machine count and remaining input parameter. The complete instance is supplied before scheduling begins. No unproved complexity assumption is included in this existence question.
cards.definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same fixed-factor approximation-existence question.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside the valid input domain. The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

Choose \(\varepsilon\), the program and its polynomial constants once, before all inputs. They cannot depend on machine count, job count, processing times or encoding precision. There is no additive slack or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; the empty instance is included.

For background notation, let \(\mathcal R\subseteq[1,\infty)\) be the set of universal multiplicative factors achievable by one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm per factor in this exact model, and put \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R\). The established factor-two algorithm makes this set nonempty. The current proposition is equivalent to \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}<2\), but does not require determining that infimum or attaining it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform deterministic algorithm with some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and the stated worst-case polynomial bit-time and feasibility guarantees, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation. Any positive constant improvement below factor two qualifies. A factor such as \(2-1/m\), whose improvement vanishes as the input machine count grows, does not qualify. Neither a guarantee for a fixed number of machines nor a restricted family of processing times settles the full target. A negative answer must exclude all positive constant improvements for all uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in this model. A conditional hardness result is only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. There is no minimum improvement of \(0.01\), and the task does not ask to determine the optimal ratio.
cards.why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.

progress.text: Lenstra–Shmoys–Tardos establish the factor-two polynomial-time algorithm, a scheme for fixed machine count, and hardness for every ratio below \(3/2\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

Bamas and coauthors prove the makespan-to-Santa-Claus reduction and the stated two-value special-case guarantees. The preprint record remains version 1.
The prediction-assisted preprint gives improved guarantees with accurate extra information and worst-case factor two. Its Theorem 5.2 retains the search-budget dependence in its running time.

cards.status_note: The individual source review of 15 September 2026 found no fixed universal improvement below two in this model. The established factor-two algorithm and conditional hardness below \(3/2\) leave different logical possibilities. Restricted-assignment algorithms, instance-dependent savings, predictions and fairness existence guarantees do not settle the unrestricted deterministic polynomial-time target. On 17 September the formulation was changed from numerical determination back to the original strict-below-two question; the earlier bounded source review and its proof-verification limits are retained.

context_blocks.text: The original source asks whether some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), independent of the instance, permits a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation. Any positive constant improvement suffices, including an improvement smaller than \(1/100\).

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee here.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
cards.definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.
cards.why: Worst-case hardness alone does not explain whether feasible procedures can generate instances that remain difficult on average. Resolving this implication would connect the central decision-class separation to robust limits on exact computation under efficiently generated inputs.

importance.reason: The foundational implication from worst-case NP hardness to feasibly generated average hardness.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The original book/survey explicitly pose the implication; inspected January and April 2026 results retain specific description-problem hardness assumptions or different distributional guarantees. The July nondeterministic-description abstract does not claim this general implication. No verified derivation from P != NP alone, or proof of its full negation, was found in bounded primary-source checks. The question remains source_open; the cited proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case intractability only says that no single polynomial-time decider works on every input. It gives no immediate frequency statement about difficult inputs under a feasible sampler. The conclusion therefore quantifies over a language together with a fixed distribution ensemble; a different hard input chosen noncomputably at each length is not an admissible sampler.

The positive-moment definition is robust under polynomial changes in running time and machine representation. Rare long computations can affect the first moment much more strongly than a smaller positive moment. Heuristics that sometimes give a wrong answer have a different success condition from the total exact deciders required here.

Distributional completeness is available for polynomial-time samplable ensembles. It identifies problems whose average tractability would imply average tractability throughout the corresponding distributional NP class. Completeness alone does not establish that this class contains a hard problem under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Likewise, easiness under a particular familiar distribution need not reflect worst-case complexity.

Bogdanov–Trevisan show that certain nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Nonadaptive means that all oracle questions are chosen before their answers are read; the reduction must work for arbitrary oracles satisfying its average-correctness promise. This restriction concerns a proof mechanism, not the truth of the unrestricted implication.

Time-bounded description complexity asks how short a program can be while producing a given string within a prescribed time. Liu–Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case connection for a deterministic description problem under an additional exponential circuit-hardness assumption. Section 5 also gives a connection for randomized description complexity without that derandomization assumption, but still assumes worst-case hardness of that particular promise problem. Neither premise has been obtained from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone in the inspected work.

The Liu–Pass paper uses AvgP for a promise-problem notion based on polynomial-time errorless heuristics, separately chosen for each inverse-polynomial failure threshold. This notation must not silently replace the single exact decider and positive-moment bound. The source review records its specific model and hypotheses rather than inferring the requested general implication from a shared class name.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s April 2026 results concern specific gap versions of description complexity, additional nonuniform hardness or derandomization assumptions, and conditional pseudorandom generators. Their hidden seed distribution can be inefficient to sample. Such a distribution does not meet the efficient sampling requirement in this question merely by existing.

cards.context:
Worst-case intractability only says that no single polynomial-time decider works on every input. It gives no immediate frequency statement about difficult inputs under a feasible sampler. The conclusion therefore quantifies over a language together with a fixed distribution ensemble; a different hard input chosen noncomputably at each length is not an admissible sampler.

The positive-moment definition is robust under polynomial changes in running time and machine representation. Rare long computations can affect the first moment much more strongly than a smaller positive moment. Heuristics that sometimes give a wrong answer have a different success condition from the total exact deciders required here.

Distributional completeness is available for polynomial-time samplable ensembles. It identifies problems whose average tractability would imply average tractability throughout the corresponding distributional NP class. Completeness alone does not establish that this class contains a hard problem under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Likewise, easiness under a particular familiar distribution need not reflect worst-case complexity.

Bogdanov–Trevisan show that certain nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Nonadaptive means that all oracle questions are chosen before their answers are read; the reduction must work for arbitrary oracles satisfying its average-correctness promise. This restriction concerns a proof mechanism, not the truth of the unrestricted implication.

Time-bounded description complexity asks how short a program can be while producing a given string within a prescribed time. Liu–Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case connection for a deterministic description problem under an additional exponential circuit-hardness assumption. Section 5 also gives a connection for randomized description complexity without that derandomization assumption, but still assumes worst-case hardness of that particular promise problem. Neither premise has been obtained from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone in the inspected work.

The Liu–Pass paper uses AvgP for a promise-problem notion based on polynomial-time errorless heuristics, separately chosen for each inverse-polynomial failure threshold. This notation must not silently replace the single exact decider and positive-moment bound. The source review records its specific model and hypotheses rather than inferring the requested general implication from a shared class name.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s April 2026 results concern specific gap versions of description complexity, additional nonuniform hardness or derandomization assumptions, and conditional pseudorandom generators. Their hidden seed distribution can be inefficient to sample. Such a distribution does not meet the efficient sampling requirement in this question merely by existing.

cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

importance.reason: The canonical statistical-computational gap supporting many average-case reductions.

progress.text: Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov obtain polynomial-time recovery for every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with a polynomial exponent that can depend on that constant.
The nearly tight sum-of-squares integrality gap first appears in 2016 and is published in SIAM Journal on Computing in 2019. It limits the specified relaxation, rather than all detection algorithms.
The final gradient-descent preprint proves recovery at a sufficiently large constant times \(\sqrt n\) from full-graph initialization, for each fixed desired error probability.
Nagda and Raghavendra’s revised paper derives optimal efficient distinguishing advantages under a hypothesis in the independent-vertex planting model.
COLT 2026 presents robust algorithms for overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs above the stated \(\sqrt{n\log n}\) scale. This is a different distribution.

A new preprint reports conditional average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation from fixed-size planted-clique detection, with a separate quantum hypothesis. This review did not independently verify its reduction.

Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving the fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\), and every integer \(q\ge\Delta+2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper labelled \(q\)-colourings satisfies \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^c?\] The constants must be independent of the graph, its degree and the number of colours. One polynomial must work uniformly over degrees and palettes; the time unit is one vertex update.
cards.definitions:
Let \(V(G)=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E(G)\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or parallel edges. Set \(N_G(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\) and \(\Delta=\max_v|N_G(v)|\). The state space is \[\Omega_{G,q}=\{\sigma:[n]\to[q]:\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E(G)\},\] where \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Colours are labelled and may be unused. There is no constraint on colour-class sizes, and no prescribed partial colouring or vertex-specific list. The state space is nonempty for the stated colour range.

At each discrete step, choose \(v\) uniformly from \([n]\). Given the current state \(\sigma\), form the available set \[A_\sigma(v)=[q]\setminus\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}.\] Choose a colour uniformly from \(A_\sigma(v)\), assign it to \(v\), and leave every other vertex unchanged. The set has at least \(q-\Delta\ge2\) elements and includes the current colour; staying in the same colouring is allowed. The choices at successive steps are made from these conditional distributions. Let \(P\) be the resulting finite stochastic matrix and let \(P^t(\sigma,\tau)\) be its \(t\)-step transition probabilities, with \(P^0\) the identity matrix. The chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi(\sigma)=1/|\Omega_{G,q}|\), the uniform law on all proper labelled colourings. In this range it is irreducible and has self-loops, so that this stationary law is approached from every state.

For probability laws \(\mu,\nu\) on the finite state space, total variation is \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu)=\frac12\sum_{\tau\in\Omega_{G,q}}|\mu(\tau)-\nu(\tau)|\). Define \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)=\min\left\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\max_{\sigma\in\Omega_{G,q}}\frac12\sum_{\tau\in\Omega_{G,q}}|P^t(\sigma,\tau)-\pi(\tau)|\le\frac14\right\}.\] One may set this minimum to infinity if the set is empty; ergodicity in the stated range ensures that it is finite. The maximum is over arbitrary initial proper colourings, with no warm-start or random-initial-state assumption.

A step updates one vertex. No factor of \(n\) is absorbed into the time unit, and uniform sampling from a potentially large colour set is part of the mathematical transition rule. Thus the statement concerns the convergence rate of a specified chain, not an implementation bound polynomial only in \(n\) for operations on \(\log q\)-bit colour names. If a graph is encoded for formalization, use its explicit vertex and edge lists and the binary integer \(q\); no succinct graph representation is intended.

The bound is simultaneous for all finite degrees and all \(q\ge\Delta+2\), including \(q\) unbounded as a function of \(n\). A theorem of the form \(C_{\Delta,q}n^{c_{\Delta,q}}\) for each fixed pair of parameters does not automatically meet it. No girth, treewidth, chordality, planarity, expansion or random-graph assumption is imposed. Girth is the shortest cycle length, with infinity for a forest. A fixed multiplicative slack \(q\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\), with \(\delta>0\), does not cover \(q=\Delta+2\) uniformly as \(\Delta\) increases.

The heat-bath convention differs from proposing a uniformly random colour from all \([q]\) and rejecting a conflict, often also called Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. In the heat-bath chain, every proposed colour is available; in the latter chain, unsuccessful proposals contribute further holding probability. Flip dynamics can recolour an entire two-colour component and is a third chain. A comparison with other mixing-time bounds must account for the update rule and time unit. The present question fixes the heat-bath chain exactly.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed uniform polynomial bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its failure. An affirmative proof must supply absolute \(C,c\) working for every graph, degree, colour count and initial proper colouring in the definition. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(C,c\) there are eligible \(n,G,q\) with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)>Cn^c\); one slow instance does not refute every polynomial. Polynomial mixing only for each fixed degree with an uncontrolled exponent, larger multiplicative palette slack, restricted graphs, a different dynamics, or an unspecified faster sampler is not the required bound. This is an exact asymptotic proposition about the specified chain, not a request to approximate a finite mixing time to the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: This tests whether the simplest local update rule samples proper colourings efficiently throughout the full range where it is guaranteed to move between all solutions. It connects random sampling, approximate counting and antiferromagnetic spin systems at a longstanding boundary for general graphs.

cards.definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le \operatorname{binom}(r,2)\operatorname{binom}(s,2)(rs \ln  2+\ln  4)\), which implies a universal polynomial bound in \(r+s\). The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this question. The claimed resolution remains uncertain because its proof has not been independently verified.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing \([[1,0],[0,1]]\) by \([[0,1],[1,0]]\) changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer the fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

cards.title: FP versus #P
cards.formal:
Is every function in \(\#\mathrm P\) computable exactly in deterministic polynomial time? With the numerical function convention defined below, the proposition is
\[\#\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N},\]
equivalently \(\#\mathrm P=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). Each function may have its own fixed machine and polynomial running-time bound. The output is the exact nonnegative integer in binary.
cards.why: This is the fundamental exact-counting analogue of P versus NP. It asks whether every efficiently checkable family of witnesses also admits efficient evaluation of its full multiplicity, and connects counting satisfiability, permanents and many discrete partition functions under one computational boundary.
cards.status_note: The January 2007 draft and the checked 2017 primary teaching sources pose the exact-counting equality as open. Bounded source searches through 16 September 2026 found no verified proof of either equality or inequality. A March 2026 preprint claiming only the conditional P = NP implication is discussed on TCS-6821; it neither asserts this unconditional equality nor supplies a valid resolution in the local proof check recorded there. This review does not certify exhaustive present openness.

cards.definitions:
Write \(\{0,1\}^*\) for all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) for their bit length. Natural numbers include zero. A polynomial witness bound is a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients; allowing any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded integer length gives the same class by unique zero padding. A verifier \(V(x,y)\) is a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine returning a bit on every pair of strings within polynomially many bit steps in \(|x|+|y|\). The class \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of the total functions
\[f_{V,p}(x)=\left|\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\right\}\right|.\]
Each distinct witness string is counted once. If several witnesses describe the same combinatorial object, their multiplicity is retained. The witness length is exactly the displayed length; shorter witnesses are not additionally counted. Equivalently, these functions count accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines with binary choices and an explicit machine convention preserving path counts.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to nonnegative integers for which some deterministic multitape Turing machine outputs the canonical binary representation on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps. Here \(C,d\) are fixed positive integers, the representation of zero is the single bit 0, and positive outputs have no leading zeros. All computation and output writing are charged. Machines have finite programs, no advice and no oracle. No error probability or approximation is allowed. The constants and program may depend on the function but never on the input. There is no requirement of a common exponent or a uniform compiler taking arbitrary verifiers as input.

Every \(\#\mathrm P\) value is at most \(2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has at most \(p(|x|)+1\) bits. The question does not request output in unary, listing all witnesses, or a time bound polynomial in the value of the count. Conversely, if a numerical function has a polynomial-time exact algorithm, choose a polynomial \(q\) longer than its output bit bound and accept a \(q(|x|)\)-bit witness precisely when its numerical value is smaller than \(f(x)\). Exactly \(f(x)\) witnesses are accepted. Thus \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm P\), which justifies writing equality rather than only the displayed inclusion. The source writes FP for this numerical interpretation of polynomial-time string functions.

For the comparisons below, \(\mathrm P\) is the class of languages decided by deterministic machines in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages of the form \(\{x:f_{V,p}(x)>0\}\). The class \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists of languages decidable using polynomially many working-tape cells, with no polynomial time restriction. A polynomial-time Turing reduction to a numerical function may make adaptively chosen exact queries, charging query writing and answer processing, while receiving the binary answer from its oracle. Counting completeness mentioned below uses this convention unless a stronger count-preserving reduction is stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\#\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\), or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must supply existence of an exact uniform polynomial-time machine for every fixed verifier and witness bound; it suffices to solve an appropriately proved counting-complete problem exactly in polynomial time. A negative proof must establish a \(\#\mathrm P\) function admitting no such machine. A conditional separation assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), a lower bound for one restricted algorithm, or an efficient relative approximation does not by itself settle the unconditional proposition. Computing only whether the count is zero is also insufficient.

source_formulation.text: Can all #P functions be computed efficiently, so that FP and #P coincide under the binary-integer convention?
source_formulation.caption: Source paraphrase of the explicit open question following Definition 9.2 in the January 2007 draft; numerical FP is made explicit.

context_blocks.text: A verifier checks one proposed witness quickly. Its counting function asks how many witnesses pass. The count can be exponentially large while its binary representation remains polynomially short, so the difficulty is not simply the time needed to write the answer.

Exact counting immediately decides whether any witness exists. Consequently, an affirmative answer implies P = NP, and a proof that P differs from NP would give a negative answer here. The converse implication is a separate question: efficient existence tests do not automatically evaluate the full count.

Counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is a representative complete problem. The usual verifier-to-formula construction can retain one satisfying assignment per accepted witness by forcing the values of auxiliary computation variables. Therefore a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm for those formulas would evaluate every function in the class.

Some counting-complete problems have easy existence tests. For a zero-one matrix, its permanent counts perfect matchings in the associated bipartite graph; testing whether such a matching exists is polynomial-time solvable. Counting completeness here is under polynomial-time oracle reductions, and does not mean a count-preserving reduction from satisfiability.

A polynomial-space computation can enumerate all witnesses while keeping only a polynomial-length counter. The textbook therefore notes that P = PSPACE would imply a positive answer. This stronger hypothesis is distinct from P = NP, and the brute-force counting procedure itself generally takes exponential time.

Relative approximation allows a nonzero error proportional to the count. When the count is exponential, even a very small inverse-polynomial relative error can hide many integers. An approximation algorithm whose running time is polynomial in inverse accuracy can need exponential time at the precision that distinguishes adjacent counts.

cards.title: FPRAS for #BIS
cards.formal: Does \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\), counting all independent sets in an arbitrary finite simple bipartite graph, admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Precisely, do there exist one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,k\geq1\) such that, for every encoded bipartite graph \(G\) and rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the machine outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) within \(C(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)^k\) steps on every random tape and satisfies \[\Pr\big[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\leq\widehat Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\big]\geq\tfrac34?\] Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of independent vertex subsets, \(L\) is the complete encoded input length, and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair coin bits.
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\geq0\), the vertex set is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), partitioned into disjoint specified sets \(U,V\), either of which may be empty. An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices with one endpoint in each part; there are no loops or parallel edges. An independent set is a subset \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) that contains no complete edge, and \(Z(G)=|\{I\subseteq U\cup V:I\text{ is independent}\}|\). Every independent set is counted once, with weight one, irrespective of its size or the number of its vertices in either part. The empty set is included, so \(Z(G)\geq1\), and the graph with no vertices has \(Z(G)=1\). Graphs may be disconnected and have isolated vertices, arbitrary degrees and parts of unequal sizes. Fix the following explicit finite-alphabet encoding. Write bin(j) for the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer j, with no leading zeros except in bin(0). An input is the string bin(n)#b#a#bin(r)#bin(s), where b has exactly n bits specifying part membership, a has exactly n(n−1)/2 bits specifying adjacency for pairs (i,j), i<j, in increasing lexicographic order, and integers r,s satisfy 0<r<s. Every adjacency bit equal to one must join vertices whose membership bits differ. The accuracy is \(\varepsilon=r/s\); the fraction need not be reduced. Thus isolated vertices are represented explicitly, and L counts all bits and separators, including both accuracy integers. The ceiling \(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\) is taken after real division. An output encodes \(\widehat Z=p/q\) as bin(p)#bin(q), with integers \(p\geq0\), \(q\geq1\). The machine has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, with a stream of independent unbiased random bits. All input reading, bit computation, random-bit access and output writing are charged as Turing-machine steps; exact arithmetic on unbounded integers or reals is not a unit-cost operation. There is no oracle, advice, quantum resource or random input-graph assumption. The same program and constants C,k must work for all graph sizes, degrees, bipartitions and accuracies. Malformed strings are rejected by returning 0/1 within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps on every random tape, after increasing the common constants if needed. Deterministic algorithms are permitted as the special case that ignores the random bits.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that a single algorithm and constants C,k meet the stated worst-case bit-cost bound, rational-output requirement and per-instance relative-error guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. The negative direction must rule out every uniform fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme. Equivalently, every candidate satisfying the polynomial runtime and output conditions must have some valid input \((G,\varepsilon)\) on which its probability of a correct relative approximation is strictly less than \(3/4\). Showing a failure of a particular sampler, a finite running-time lower bound, or difficulty of exact counting does not establish this universal impossibility. A conditional lower bound, for example one assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), is not an unconditional negative resolution unless the assumed separation is also proved. The positive direction must cover every input graph and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with a polynomial degree independent of those inputs; expected runtime alone does not match the specified bound without a proof yielding the required always-bounded scheme. The target is existence of an approximation algorithm with its requested accuracy parameter, so a fixed numerical tolerance of 1/100 does not replace the quantified relative-error requirement. A deterministic fully polynomial scheme would meet the target, but is not required.
cards.why: The canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting: many counting problems share its approximation difficulty, while exact counting hardness does not settle whether a randomized relative approximation is efficient. A general scheme would transfer to problems reducible to it with preserved approximation guarantees; an impossibility proof would separate this central family from the counting problems with known fully polynomial schemes.

context_blocks.text: An independent set need not be maximal or maximum. For an edgeless graph on \(n\) vertices the count is \(2^n\), whereas a complete bipartite graph with part sizes \(a,b\) has \(2^a+2^b-1\) independent sets: any subset of either part is allowed, with the empty set counted only once. In every bipartite graph all subsets of each part are independent, so the count can be exponentially large even though the instance and the binary representation of its count have polynomial length. The requested error is relative to that count, not to the number of vertices.

Exact counting and approximate counting have different known boundaries. The 2019 primary source recalls that exact \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete even at maximum degree three, while efficient relative approximation is known when all degrees on one side are at most five. It also recalls that allowing maximum degree six already recovers the full approximation difficulty. Here \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of counts of accepting computation paths of nondeterministic polynomial-time machines; hardness of computing such counts exactly does not itself rule out an FPRAS.

Approximation-preserving reductions allow a counting problem to be solved using relative approximations for another, with polynomial overhead and polynomially controlled requested precision. The literature contains many problems equivalent to \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) under such reductions, including problems about constrained assignments and statistical-mechanics models. The 2019 authors describe the family as conjecturally intermediate: neither an FPRAS nor NP-hardness of approximation is known for the unrestricted target. This is a description of the open complexity landscape, not a proved impossibility theorem.

The hard-core partition function is \(Z_G(\lambda)=\sum_{I\text{ independent}}\lambda^{|I|}\), for a positive parameter \(\lambda\) called fugacity. It normalizes the probability distribution assigning each independent set probability \(\lambda^{|I|}/Z_G(\lambda)\). The fugacity is \(\lambda=1\), so every independent set has equal weight. Results for other fugacities or for distributions conditioned on a prescribed set size must be checked against this unweighted total count.

Liao, Lin, Lu and Mao give an FPTAS for almost every \(\Delta\)-regular bipartite graph when the fixed degree \(\Delta\geq53\), including the unweighted count. Regular means that every vertex has the same degree. Their probability is over a uniformly chosen graph with \(n\) vertices on each side, and tends to one as \(n\to\infty\); the approximation algorithm itself is deterministic. This is a substantial result for typical inputs, but it does not guarantee success on every bipartite graph as required here.

The ICALP 2024 dense-graph theorem gives an FPRAS for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\) on graphs with \(2n\) vertices that are \(\lfloor\delta n\rfloor\)-regular. Its constants and polynomial running-time degree may depend on the fixed density \(\delta\). Consequently, allowing \(\delta\) to decrease with the input size does not turn the stated theorem into a fully polynomial bound for all bipartite graphs. The paper’s exponential-form relative error and the \(1\pm\varepsilon\) convention are equivalent for the existence of an FPRAS after a constant-factor change in the accuracy parameter.

The August 2026 preprint studies a different count: only independent sets occupying the two sides equally, or prescribed numbers of vertices on the two sides. Theorem 1.2 reports an approximation hardness threshold for the balanced partition function. In particular, at fugacity one and maximum degree six, it reports no FPRAS unless \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}\). Here NP is nondeterministic polynomial time, and RP is randomized polynomial-time decision with no false positives and acceptance probability at least one half on positive instances. The balance restriction changes which sets are counted, so this conditional result does not establish hardness of the unrestricted total count here. The new proof has not been independently verified.

The same August preprint explicitly states that ordinary \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) is neither known to admit an FPRAS nor known to be NP-hard to approximate. A slow-mixing Markov chain is likewise an obstruction to that chain, rather than to all possible randomized approximation algorithms. The remaining question concerns the existence of any uniform scheme satisfying the full worst-case guarantee.
