All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes the test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis here. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

benchmark_focus.reason: Complete EFX existence is a central feasibility question for fairness with indivisible goods and unrestricted agent counts.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
cards.definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.
cards.why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

importance.reason: Constant-factor truthful submodular auctions would determine whether exact incentives impose an unbounded welfare loss.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected general upper guarantee remains \(O((\log\log m)^2)\) with universal truthfulness and expected welfare. Value-query lower bounds do not cover arbitrary communication. The February 2026 graph-auction theorem and August procurement claims have distinct restrictions or type spaces. No matching constant-factor resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; complete cited proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand answer can describe a preferred bundle in \(m\) bits even if finding it requires comparing exponentially many bundles. The price vector must also be sent and paid for in the communication bound. This explains why a communication-efficient mechanism can delegate difficult optimization to a bidder without being computationally efficient for that bidder. It also explains why a bound on the number of queries alone is not a complete bit-cost specification.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla’s FOCS 2019 result gives a universally truthful expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) welfare approximation with polynomially many queries. The later journal publication records the same advance, rather than a new constant-factor result. These approximation factors are asymptotic as the number of items grows.

Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla’s Theorem 2 improves the expected approximation factor for submodular and XOS bidders to \(O((\log\log m)^2)\), using at most one value or demand query per bidder. For the broader subadditive class the guarantee is \(O((\log\log m)^3)\). The theorem is universally truthful. The squared iterated logarithm still diverges, so it does not supply the fixed constant sought here.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

An August 2026 preprint claims constant budget-feasible approximations with demand queries. Its buyer purchases services from sellers with private participation costs under a payment budget. That is a different type space and objective from allocating items among bidders with private submodular bundle values. The result therefore does not resolve this question, even though both settings use truthfulness and submodularity.

cards.title: VP versus VNP
cards.formal:
Over the complex field \(\mathbb C\), do there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some arithmetic circuit with at most \(B(n+1)^k\) operation gates computes the permanent polynomial
\[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}\ \in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]?\]
Circuits are division-free, have binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates, allow arbitrary complex constants and unrestricted reuse, and compute exact formal polynomials. No uniform construction of the circuits is required. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), with the classes defined below? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
cards.definitions:
Polynomial and parameter. For \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(S_n\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) consists of \(n^2\) independent commuting indeterminates. The displayed sum has one product for each permutation; each product chooses one variable in each row and column. Its total degree is \(n\). The growing parameter in the size bound is the matrix dimension \(n\), not the number of monomials or the magnitude of a numerical input. The number of input variables is \(N=n^2\).

Circuit model. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a distinguished output node. Each input node carries either one of the indeterminates or one exact constant from \(\mathbb C\). Each other node has two ordered incoming wires and a label \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\); the same preceding node may feed both incoming wires. A node is evaluated in the commutative polynomial ring by applying its operation to the polynomials at its two predecessors. An input node itself may be the output. The circuit's size \(s(D)\) is the number of operation nodes; input nodes are not counted. A computed value may feed arbitrarily many subsequent nodes at no additional gate cost. Cancellations are allowed. Neither depth nor the degrees of intermediate polynomials are restricted. All constants are freely selected as part of the finite circuit and may depend on \(n\); their numerical bit lengths, descriptions or computability are not charged. Each arithmetic operation costs one gate. This is an arithmetic circuit measure, not a Turing-machine bit-time model. Input constants supply no operation other than their fixed field value: there are no bit-extraction, comparison, branching, oracle or division gates. Approximation and limits of circuits are also outside this model.

Exact computation and families. A circuit computes \(f\) when its output equals \(f\) as an element of the polynomial ring, meaning that every monomial has the same coefficient. Agreement at a selected finite set of matrices is not the correctness definition. Let \(c_{\mathbb C}(f)\) be the minimum size of such a circuit for \(f\). Every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum is a nonnegative integer. In the main question the quantifier order is
\[\exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists D_n:\quad s(D_n)\le B(n+1)^k,\quad D_n\text{ computes }\operatorname{perm}_n.\]
The constants \(B,k\) are shared across all matrix dimensions. The circuits themselves may be unrelated from one dimension to the next: no machine, advice-generation procedure or polynomial-time algorithm for producing them is part of the assertion. Restricting constants to integers or rationals, or asking for a uniform family, would change this selected model.

Complexity classes. A sequence \(a(n)\) of nonnegative integers is polynomially bounded if some integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfy \(a(n)\le B(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). A polynomial family is a sequence \((m(n),f_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(m(n)\ge0\) and \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\); both \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_n\) must be polynomially bounded. Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; for this boundedness condition give the zero polynomial degree zero. The family lies in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) if \(c_{\mathbb C}(f_n)\) is polynomially bounded as well, using the circuit model above. These are bounds on the resulting polynomials, not extra syntactic degree bounds at circuit gates.

Such a family lies in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if there are a polynomially bounded witness length \(w(n)\in\mathbb N\) and a family
\[g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)},y_1,\ldots,y_{w(n)}]\]
in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\), with combined variable counts and total degrees polynomially bounded in \(n\), such that
\[f_n(x)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{w(n)}}g_n(x,a).\]
Each Boolean witness is embedded into \(\mathbb C^{w(n)}\) using the field elements zero and one; the sum is a finite algebraic sum over exactly those witnesses, not an existential quantifier and not a sum over all complex tuples. If \(w(n)=0\), there is one empty witness, so \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\). No uniformity is imposed on these families or their circuit constants. Class equality means equality of these collections of polynomial families.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish common integers \(B,k\ge1\) and an appropriate finite circuit for every \(n\), with exact polynomial identity and the size bound in this model. A uniform construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative answer must prove
\[\forall B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad c_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)>B(n+1)^k.\]
Equivalently, the violating dimension can be required to exceed any specified lower threshold, since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed into the coefficient \(B\). The lower bound must cover every finite circuit with arbitrary complex constants, cancellations and reuse. A result proved via the class-equality formulation must include the equivalence to this concrete permanent target. A fixed polynomial lower bound, even superlinear in \(n^2\), is insufficient to prove the negation. Lower bounds confined to formulas, monotone circuits, fixed depth, or superpolynomial determinantal complexity do not by themselves establish the required general-circuit separation. A numerical approximation scheme, a border-limit construction, or a result only over another field does not supply the exact circuits quantified here.
cards.why: This is the central equality question for general arithmetic computation. It asks whether a polynomial-size algebraic computation can always absorb a sum over exponentially many Boolean witnesses, with the permanent serving as a complete concrete target. A separation would establish a general limitation despite arbitrary constants, cancellations and reuse; equality would give polynomial-size circuits for every polynomial family in VNP.

context_blocks.text: The permanent of a matrix sums the weights of its perfect matchings when rows and columns form the two sides of a bipartite graph. For a zero-one matrix it counts perfect matchings. Already in dimension two, \(\operatorname{perm}_2(X)=x_{11}x_{22}+x_{12}x_{21}\), while the determinant subtracts the second product. The question concerns the symbolic polynomial for all complex inputs.

The determinant contains the same permutation products with signs, yet has polynomial-size division-free circuits. Thus factorially many displayed terms do not force factorial circuit size. Reusing expressions and canceling terms are central powers of the model. Counting perfect matchings on binary inputs is a related Boolean counting problem, but that bit-complexity problem is not the same as allowing arbitrary complex constants at unit arithmetic cost.

Valiant’s completeness theorem makes the permanent universal for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over fields of characteristic different from two. Each VNP family can be obtained from a polynomially larger permanent by substituting variables and field constants. This establishes the equivalence in the question over \(\mathbb C\). The field choice matters: in characteristic two the permanent and determinant coincide.

Ryser’s identity gives an exponential-size upper bound, including formulas using \(O(n^2 2^n)\) arithmetic operations. In contrast, a positive answer here requires one fixed polynomial bound for all dimensions. A formula is a circuit whose intermediate results cannot be shared; forbidding reuse can substantially increase the needed size.

Limaye, Srinivasan and Tavenas proved superpolynomial lower bounds for every constant circuit depth over characteristic-zero fields. Their hard polynomial is an iterated matrix product entry, which itself has polynomial-size unrestricted circuits. The low-depth theorem therefore illustrates the power of removing a depth restriction rather than proving VP different from VNP. The result first appeared in 2021 and was published in the Journal of the ACM in 2025.

The 1 August 2026 OpenAI manuscript reports a lower bound \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) for unrestricted division-free circuits computing the permanent, and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) for formulas, including formulas with valid divisions. The circuit model in Chapter 5 matches this question, but the bound is still polynomial in matrix dimension and hence does not separate VP and VNP. The release supplies Lean certificates; this review checked the mathematical statements and repository description without replaying or independently auditing those certificates.

Narayanan’s work, published on ECCC on 9 August 2026 after a July submission, reports improved superlinear lower bounds for certain sublogarithmic depths and explicit elusive curves of exponential degree. The manuscript explicitly explains that its current parameters do not establish VP different from VNP. These are results with stated depth and degree qualifications, not a general superpolynomial permanent lower bound.

A determinantal representation expresses a polynomial as \(\det A(x)\), where every matrix entry is an affine linear form in its variables. Its minimum matrix dimension measures a more restricted representation than an arbitrary arithmetic circuit. A superpolynomial bound on that dimension alone does not settle this question; polynomial-size general circuits can be simulated by determinantal representations of quasipolynomial size. Exact representation must also be distinguished from taking limits of such representations.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint gives deterministic polynomial bit-time approximation of the permanent of nonnegative rational matrices within a factor \(\exp(O(n(\log\log n)^2/\log n))\). This is a recent algorithmic advance for numerical approximate counting. Its input restriction and multiplicative-error guarantee do not give exact formal-polynomial circuits over \(\mathbb C\).

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position \((i,j)\) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly \(c_{ij}\), so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define \(s(n)\) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and \(C>0\) there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The conjecture \(\omega=2\) predicts one possible value of the target exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.
cards.why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity here permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).

Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity here permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).

benchmark_focus.reason: The matrix multiplication exponent governs a fundamental operation and propagates to a broad range of algorithms.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

importance.reason: Rational Diophantine decidability is a landmark boundary between arithmetic, computability and algebraic geometry.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by \(\operatorname{code}(r)\) and then \(\operatorname{code}(p_i),\operatorname{code}(e_i)\) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: Classical polynomial-time factoring is a central arithmetic complexity question with broad cryptographic and quantum-computing consequences.

progress.text: Shor establishes polynomial-time quantum factorization. The full paper’s January 1996 revision explicitly uses quantum computation, which is outside the classical randomized machine model of this question.
Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena publish deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. This makes prime-factor lists efficiently checkable but does not provide their discovery.

Harvey and Hittmeir prove complete deterministic factorization in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log N)^{16/5}/(\log\log N)^{3/5})\) bit operations as N tends to infinity. The 2022 journal result improves a logarithmic factor while retaining an exponential dependence on binary input length.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revision removes the previous power-of-N lower restriction on the large-order threshold and slightly improves its runtime factor. Theorem 1.1 may return a large-order element instead of a divisor, and Section 1.1 still explicitly identifies polynomial-time factoring as unknown.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.
Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
cards.definitions:
Finite codes. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), a binary length-\(n\) code is a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\). Its elements are codewords. For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), define their Hamming distance by
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
The distance requirement means \(d_H(x,y)\ge d\) for every distinct pair \(x,y\in C\). A singleton satisfies it vacuously; no minimum over an empty set needs to be chosen. Define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall x,y\in C,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow d_H(x,y)\ge d\}.\]
This is a finite maximum over a nonempty collection, and \(1\le A_2(n,d)\le2^n\). The rate of \(C\) is \(r(C)=\log_2|C|/n\). The distance parameter \(d/n\) is a required relative separation, not the fraction of independent random channel errors. All logarithms are base two.

Asymptotic convention. Fix the real parameter \(\delta\) before taking the block length to infinity. The integer \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the smallest integer at least \(\delta n\). For \(0\le\delta\le1\), write \(a_n(\delta)=\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)/n\). Explicitly,
\[R_2(\delta)=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\ \sup_{n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge N} a_n(\delta).\]
Every term is in \([0,1]\), so the tail suprema and infimum are well-defined finite real numbers. The limsup allows a favorable infinite subsequence of block lengths and does not assert that the ordinary limit exists. The optimum ranges over all codes, without linearity or a single effective code-family generator. The requested domain is exactly \((0,1/2)\); the same definition outside it gives the known regimes \(R_2(0)=1\) and \(R_2(\delta)=0\) for \(1/2\le\delta\le1\).

Conventions for bounds. A lower curve \(L\) satisfies \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a valid code of length \(n\), distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\), and rate at least \(L(\delta)-\varepsilon\). An upper curve \(U\) satisfies \(R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) has the following property: for every \(n\ge N\), every valid code at that distance has rate at most \(U(\delta)+\varepsilon\). Block length thresholds may depend on \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\); a common threshold for all real distances is not required. These existence bounds do not impose polynomial-time code construction.

For the background bounds, the binary entropy is \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) on \([0,1]\), with each endpoint term \(0\log_2 0\) interpreted as zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified function \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(|g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le1/100\) for every real \(\delta\) in that domain, using the finite-code maximum, rounding, limsup and normalization above. This requires both \(g(\delta)-1/100\le R_2(\delta)\) and \(R_2(\delta)\le g(\delta)+1/100\); the preceding quantified code statements specify the corresponding lower and upper guarantees. Alternatively, certified curves \(L,U\) satisfying \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) everywhere qualify through their midpoint. A formula, certified evaluation rule or another unambiguous mathematical description may specify the answer; no predetermined formula grammar or evaluation-time bound is imposed. Merely renaming the defining optimization or limsup does not supply the requested determination. An exact determination qualifies, but exact equality to the Gilbert–Varshamov curve is not required. Finitely many samples, an uncertified numerical plot, a bound on only one side, or a result restricted to linear codes or to some distances does not establish the stated whole-domain guarantee.
cards.why: This function is the intrinsic packing limit for binary information protected against worst-case substitutions. Determining it to a certified rate accuracy would quantify the necessary redundancy independently of how a code is represented, constructed or decoded. Exact determination would settle a foundational coding-theory question; the selected tolerance is a distinct, weaker benchmark target.

context_blocks.text: A code represents messages by selected bit strings. More codewords carry more information per transmitted bit, while greater pairwise separation permits correction of more adversarial errors. This question asks for the best possible asymptotic compromise over every binary code, independently of algorithmic restrictions.

The repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, and corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The complete set of three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, and cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. In general, correction of every pattern of at most \(t\) substitutions requires and is guaranteed by pairwise distance at least \(2t+1\), for an integer \(t\ge0\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov existence bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\ge1-h_2(\delta)\), whereas the elementary Hamming bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\le1-h_2(\delta/2)\). Vadhan’s Open Problem 5.9 asks for the largest asymptotically attainable binary rate at a fixed relative distance. Its infinite-family formulation is represented here by the explicit limsup and subsequence convention.

The 1977 McEliece–Rodemich–Rumsey–Welch bounds sharpen the upper side. The first gives \(R_2(\delta)\le h_2(1/2-\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)})\); the second is never weaker. These were the long-standing general upper bounds, but the August 2026 preprints report strict improvements, so the 1977 frontier must not be described as current.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s 10 August 2026 preprint reports strict improvements to the first and second MRRW bounds at every \(0<\delta<1/2\). The theorems concern arbitrary classical binary codes, including nonlinear ones; quantum states occur in the analysis and do not change the code alphabet. The introduction still identifies the GV curve as the best general asymptotic lower bound.

The requested tolerance needs a separate check from exact openness. At relative distance one quarter, the GV rate is approximately 0.18872, while Table 2 of the August preprint reports a numerical upper-bound estimate near 0.35038. The authors explicitly label the table as floating-point evaluations, not certified global optima. These reported values illustrate the remaining difference between the displayed lower and upper estimates; they are not a certified interval or a proof that no different approximation theorem exists. The checked sources do not supply the requested error of 0.01 throughout the domain.

Barg’s 1 September 2026 note compares the new channel bound with the concurrent Delsarte-certificate result. Its Section 2 identifies the coinciding variational formulas for the improvement of the first MRRW bound. The note provides a mathematical relation between those results, rather than a determination of the full rate–distance function.

Finite-length improvements can leave the limiting rate unchanged. Jiang and Vardy obtain a factor of order \(n\) over the binary Gilbert bound for each fixed \(0<\delta\le0.499\). Such a multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log n/n)\) after taking the logarithm and dividing by block length. It does not constitute an increase in the asymptotic rate exponent.

Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a probabilistic proof of a square-root block-length improvement for linear codes and an extension to quantum codes. The paper acknowledges the earlier classical square-root improvement. These polynomial factors do not by themselves alter \(R_2\), and the quantum-code statement has different objects and constraints.

Capacity under independent random bit flips, list decoding, and codes over larger alphabets have different targets. The question asks for worst-case pairwise separation over the binary alphabet. A construction above the GV curve at even one distance would address the separate beyond-GV question, while this question requires two-sided accuracy over the entire distance interval.

cards.title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
cards.formal:
Determine the function
\[F(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for every finite discrete memoryless broadcast channel \(W\) with a rational transition table and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]\). Here \(C(W)\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, deterministic codes, vanishing joint average decoding error, and no feedback, as defined below. The required accuracy is absolute \(1/100\) bit per channel use throughout this entire domain.
cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\). The domain contains all positive integers \(a,b,c\), alphabets \(\mathcal X=[a]\), \(\mathcal Y=[b]\), \(\mathcal Z=[c]\), and arrays \(W(y,z\mid x)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) such that \(\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y,z\in\mathcal Z}W(y,z\mid x)=1\) for every \(x\). Alphabet sizes are unbounded, and zero transition probabilities are allowed. There is no conditional-independence requirement on the two outputs in a single use. For each block length \(n\ge1\), the channel law is
\[\Pr(Y^{n}=y^{n},Z^{n}=z^{n}\mid X^{n}=x^{n})=\prod_{t=1}^{n}W(y_{t},z_{t}\mid x_{t}).\]
The table specifies the whole channel; it has no additional state or memory.

An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code, with positive integer message sizes, consists of maps \(f:[K_{1}]\times[K_{2}]\to\mathcal X^{n}\), \(d_{1}:\mathcal Y^{n}\to[K_{1}]\), and \(d_{2}:\mathcal Z^{n}\to[K_{2}]\). The messages \(M_{1},M_{2}\) are independent and uniform, the encoder transmits \(f(M_{1},M_{2})\), and the receivers output \(d_{1}(Y^{n})\) and \(d_{2}(Z^{n})\). Its joint average error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Z^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
where the probability averages over both messages and the specified channel randomness. No worst-case-over-messages error requirement is imposed. The encoder knows both messages; each decoder observes only its own output block. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, shared randomness, secrecy condition, or input-cost constraint. Codes are arbitrary deterministic maps with no uniform construction or complexity bound. Dependence among the transmitted symbols and deterministic time sharing are allowed.

All logarithms defining rates have base two; rates and the target function are measured in bits per channel use. A pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes, indexed by \(j\ge1\), with \(n_{j}\to\infty\), \(P_{e,j}\to0\), and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}\log_{2}(K_{i,j})/n_{j}\ge R_{i}\) for both \(i=1,2\). Define \(C(W)\) as the Euclidean closure of the achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,\log_{2}b]\times[0,\log_{2}c]\); these properties and the endpoint weights make \(F\) a finite real function, including when an alphabet has size one. A supremum in the definition does not require a finite code attaining a boundary rate. Its exact values at all rational weights determine the closed region; the benchmark below requires only their stated approximation.

If an answer is given as an algorithm, its finite input is the three alphabet sizes followed by the full table in lexicographic order and the weight, with integers in binary and rational numbers as reduced numerator/positive-denominator pairs separated by delimiters. All valid inputs in this encoding are included. No time bound or fixed grammar for a mathematical answer is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire domain above and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[\forall W\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1],\qquad |g(W,\lambda)-F(W,\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must match the code model, average error, limiting convention, units, and unbounded range of alphabet sizes. It must justify both sides of the error guarantee against the operational capacity definition. Certified bounds \(L(W,\lambda)\le F(W,\lambda)\le U(W,\lambda)\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. An exact determination also qualifies. Any submitted evaluation algorithm must terminate for every valid input and certify its returned value; a mathematical expression is not required to have a prescribed computational complexity. Sampled agreement, an uncertified numerical optimizer, a one-sided achievable or converse bound, and a renaming of the defining supremum or an unevaluated limiting characterization do not suffice. Resolving whether one particular inner bound is exact is not by itself the requested function, and an impossibility result for a different evaluation task does not replace this answer.
cards.why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.

importance.reason: General broadcast capacity is a defining unresolved law for communicating independent information to multiple receivers.

progress.text: Marton gives a general achievable region for independent private messages and identifies special capacity cases.

The checked v3 of Gohari–Anantharam gives auxiliary-cardinality bounds, closedness and computability of the inner region, and a mismatch with a known outer region; the journal publication followed in 2012.
Geng and coauthors obtain capacity for new product-channel classes and show that the UV outer bound can be loose.
Dou and coauthors publish numerical bound-evaluation algorithms with convergence guarantees under specified concavity and initialization conditions.
The checked Gohari–Liu–Nair full manuscript gives stronger outer bounds and example improvements; it still describes general capacity as unknown.

Huang–Liu–Liu v1 claims a finite unconstrained counterexample to full one-letter Marton optimality, including an explicit rational enlarged channel. This narrower claim is not an independently verified capacity solution.

context_blocks.text: One transmitter must convey two independent messages through a single stream of inputs. Each receiver sees its own noisy observations, so the possible pairs of reliable rates form a tradeoff region. Unlike an interference channel, there are no separately informed transmitters. This is a central network information theory question because even the general two-receiver case lacks a known evaluable capacity characterization in the checked sources.

The two individual capacities do not determine the joint region. If the same noiseless input bit reaches both receivers, either receiver alone can receive one bit per use, but the private rates satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le1\). If the input is instead a pair of bits and each receiver receives its designated bit, the region is \([0,1]^{2}\), although both individual capacities are still one. These examples distinguish the shared resource in the question from two independent point-to-point capacity calculations.

Marton’s 1979 region is a general achievable inner bound, and the original paper identifies channel classes for which capacity is known. Its two independent private messages match this question. The original separate average-error requirements and the vanishing probability that either decoder fails are equivalent by elementary probability bounds; neither is the maximal-message error criterion.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite bounds on the auxiliary alphabet sizes in Marton’s inner region, making that region closed and computable. Their formulation permits a common message; setting its rate to zero gives the private-message slice relevant here. They also establish that this inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region can differ. This gap alone does not identify which bound is loose, and computability of an inner region does not establish its equality with capacity.

Geng and coauthors determine capacity for certain product-channel classes and prove that the UV outer bound is not always tight. Their full version also explains the multiletter sum-rate characterization: normalized Marton sum rates on successively longer repeated channels recover the operational sum capacity in the limit. This limiting equality supplies no general finite stopping guarantee for the numerical answer requested here. Nonadditivity of Marton’s inner bound must not be confused with a failure of the usual rate normalization for repeated uses of the channel itself.

Dou and coauthors give numerical methods for evaluating several inner and outer bounds. Their Theorems 5–7 prove convergence under explicit hypotheses: the initial distribution and a global maximizer must lie in a suitable connected superlevel set, and the objective must be concave there. These are conditional convergence results, not an unconditional global capacity evaluator. Even exact optimization of a bound would still leave the issue of its tightness. Their numerical conventions use natural logarithms unless otherwise specified; the target uses bits throughout.

Gohari, Liu and Nair’s 2026 manuscript strengthens sum-rate outer bounds through two auxiliary receivers, with a full-region version in its appendix and numerical improvements for skew-symmetric examples. The auxiliary receivers are proof variables, not extra terminals available to a code. The reported improvements still leave inner/outer gaps and do not give the general function.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s preprint of 20 August 2026 claims strict suboptimality of the complete one-letter Marton region. A fixed-input-distribution example has ternary input; their separate constraint-removal theorem and explicit construction produce an unconstrained channel on a much larger finite alphabet. Section III.D specifies rational mixing probabilities and a rational joint channel, so that example is within the domain. It should not be described as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample. The claim concerns a gap from an inner bound, not a matching capacity evaluation. Its full proof and interval-arithmetic certificates were not independently verified or rerun.

Approximation at the stated tolerance does not require exact equality with a proposed capacity curve. Historical open-status statements about exact capacity alone do not establish that this approximation target remains unsolved.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

Fiat–Ron give polynomial-query distance approximation for induced P3-freeness, induced P4-freeness and chordality; their induced C4 result has exponential reciprocal-accuracy dependence.
Gishboliner–Kushnir–Shapira improve the general and hereditary conversion bounds. Theorem 1.9 still has a double-exponential loss and does not prove polynomial preservation.
The survey records the stronger quantitative conversion as Problem 5.4 and describes positive special cases after it.

context_blocks.text: A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this question, but a proof of this question would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

cards.title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. Polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension is required at each fixed accuracy; no polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required.

cards.why: Gaussian mixtures are a basic example where enough observations can be available but extracting a useful distribution from them may remain computationally difficult. Joint dependence on dimension and component count distinguishes scalable learning from methods efficient only for a small fixed mixture. Resolving this target would clarify that statistical–computational gap in the absence of separation or conditioning assumptions.

On 16 September 2026 the full source definitions and question, the 2017 and 2022 hardness manuscripts, the November 2024 score-matching theorem, and the April 2025/August 2026 primary abstracts were checked. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution of the stated target. The output must be proper; fixed-accuracy quantifiers and exact-real primitives specify an arithmetic-complexity question, not a bit-complexity theorem. Conditional hardness and restricted-model lower bounds remain qualified. Cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.
